Management of the process may be decentralized, making it more flexible and responsive to market needs. This type of organization is best suited to companies whose dominant orientation is to a market or consumer group and where flexibility and innovation are more important than coordinated planning. See: process-focused organization.
A type of operation designed to process only a few different products, which are usually produced for inventory. Production rates tend to be greater than the demand rate.
The conversion of inputs into finished products.

The function of routing and dispatching the work to be accomplished through the production facility and of performing supplier control. PAC encompasses the principles, approaches, and techniques needed to schedule, control, measure, and evaluate the effectiveness of production operations. See: shop floor control.

General term referring to the body of knowledge and activities concerned with planning and controlling rates of purchasing, production, distribution, and related capacity resources to achieve target levels of customer service; backlogs; operating costs; inventory investment; manufacturing efficiency; and ultimately, profit and return on investment.
The management of an organization’s production of goods or services.
Syn.: shop calendar.

1) The highest sustainable output rate that could be achieved for a given product mix, raw materials, worker effort, plant, and equipment. 2) The collection of personnel, equipment, material, and process segment capabilities. 3) The total of the current committed, available, and unattainable capability of the production facility. The capability includes the capacity of the resource.
A card or other signal for indicating that items should be made for use or that some items removed from pipeline stock should be replaced. See: kanban.
The function of directing or regulating the movement of goods through the entire manufacturing cycle from the requisitioning of raw material to the delivery of the finished products.
The set of activities that occur during the creation of a finished good from raw materials or subassemblies.

An element of manufacturing strategy that defines the span of an operation by addressing the following areas: (1) the established boundaries for the firm’s activities; (2) the construction of supply chain relationships outside the firm’s boundaries; (3) circumstances under which changes in established boundaries or relationships are necessary; and (4) the effect of such boundary or relationship changes on the firm’s competitive position. See: manufacturing strategy.
Syn.: manufacturing environment.

A projected level of customer demand for a feature (option, accessory, etc.) of a make-to-order (MTO) or an assemble-to-order (ATO) product. Used in two-level master scheduling, it is calculated by netting customer backlog against an overall family or product line master production schedule (MPS) and then factoring this product’s available-to-promise (ATP) by the option percentage in a planning bill of material (BOM). See: assemble-to-order (ATO), planning bill of material (BOM), two-level master schedule.
A signal, usually a card, used to trigger the production of a part.
Syn.: manufacturing lead time.
Syn.: production rate.
Syn.: level production method.
Pieces of equipment or processes dedicated to the manufacture of a specific type of products or product families. See: assembly line, product layout.
Ordering, shipping, receiving, and staging materials in the same sequence they will be used.
A group of materials that is processed in one stage of production and put in inventory for further production or for shipment to customers. See: batch.

1) The planning, scheduling, execution, and control of the process of converting inputs into finished goods. 2) A field of study that focuses on the effective planning, scheduling, use, and control of a manufacturing organization. It examines concepts from design engineering, industrial engineering, management information systems, quality management, inventory management, accounting, and other functions to determine how they affect the transformation process.
Any material used in the manufacturing process.
Syn.: material requisition.

All work centers, processes, and inventory points, from raw materials sequentially to finished products and product families. It represents the logical system that provides the framework to attain the strategic objectives of the firm based on its resources and the products’ volumes and processes. It also provides the general sequential flow and capacity requirement relationships among raw materials, parts, resources, and product families.
Syn.: manufacturing order.

A technique, primarily used in the automotive and aerospace industries, that outlines requirements for approval of production parts. Its purpose is to establish confidence in the supply chain by measuring whether a supplier can fulfill these requirements with regularity.

The agreed-upon plan that comes from the production planning (sales and operations planning (S&OP)) process, which provides the overall level of planned manufacturing output, usually stated as a monthly rate for each product family. The plan represents management’s authorization for the master scheduler to convert it into the more detailed master production schedule (MPS). Syn.: operations plan. See: sales plan.

The process of developing tactical plans based on setting the overall level of manufacturing output in the production plan, as well as other activities to best satisfy the current planned levels of sales, while meeting general business objectives of profitability, productivity, competitive customer lead times, etc., as expressed in the overall business plan. See: tactical planning.

An element of manufacturing strategy that includes the design and development of manufacturing planning and control (MPC) systems in relation to the following considerations: (1) market- related criteria—the required level of delivery speed and reliability in a given market segment; (2) process requirement criteria—consistency between process type and the production planning and control system; and (3) organization control levels—systems for providing long-term planning and short-term control capabilities for strategic and operational considerations by management. See: manufacturing strategy.

The approach taken in setting the overall manufacturing output to meet customer demand by setting production levels, inventory levels, and backlog. See: chase production method, hybrid production method, level production method.
The activities involved in converting inputs into finished goods. See: manufacturing process, transformation process.
The rate of production usually expressed in units, cases, or some other broad measure, expressed by a period of time (e.g., per hour, shift, day, or week). Syn.: production level.
Syn.: manufacturing order.

A statement of the output of a production facility for a specified period. The information normally includes the type and quantity of output, work center efficiencies and utilization, costs of direct labor, direct material, any overtime worked, and machine downtime.

A process for providing feedback to the production schedule and allow for corrective action and maintenance of valid on-hand and on-order balances. It normally includes manufacturing order authorization, release, acceptance, operation start, delay reporting, move reporting, scrap and rework reporting, order close-out, and payroll interface. Syns.: manufacturing order reporting, shop order reporting.
A plan that authorizes the production facility to manufacture a certain quantity of a specific item. It is usually initiated by the production planning department.
The process of developing the production schedule.
A time standard to produce piece parts and assemblies.
A process that transforms resources into goods and services.
The time required to manufacture a product, including setup time and the processing time per piece multiplied by the number of pieces. See: manufacturing lead time.
Activities that confirm that a process will consistently produce output that meets quality standards.

In theory of constraints, the maximum of the output capabilities of a resource (or series of resources) or the market demand for that output for a given time period. See: excess capacity, idle capacity, protective capacity.
In theory of constraints, the inventory required to meet production requirements without allowance for unplanned delays. See: idle inventory, protective inventory.

1) An overall measure of the ability to produce a good or a service. It is the actual output of production compared with the actual input of resources. Productivity is a relative measure across time or against common entities (labor, capital, etc.). One example is a ratio that is calculated by adding the dollar value of labor, capital equipment, energy, and material, and so forth and dividing it into the dollar value of output in a given time period. This is one measure of total factor productivity. See: efficiency, labor productivity, machine productivity, utilization. 2) In economics, the ratio of output in terms of dollars of sales to an input such as direct labor in terms of the total wages. This is also known as single factor productivity (SFP) or partial-factor productivity.
The ability to change over quickly to other products produced in a facility, as required by demand shifts in mix.
Locating operations close to the sources of supply. See: market-positioned strategy.
A warehouse located close to the manufacturing plants that acts as a consolidation point for products.
The difference between the amount earned and the amount spent. See: gross profit, net profit, operating profit.

An area of a company that has the ability to affect both the revenues earned and the costs incurred by and allocated to the center. Operational effectiveness is evaluated in terms of the amount of profit generated.

1) For an organization, net income divided by revenue. Syn.: net profit margin. 2) For a product, (selling price - product cost) / selling price. The product cost includes both direct and indirect costs.
A plan by which employees receive compensation above their normal wages based on company profitability. The purpose is to motivate employees and recognize their efforts.
A measure of the excess income over expenditure during a given period of time.

In activity-based cost accounting, the examination of profit received from cost objects to attempt to optimize profitability. A variety of views may be examined, including customer, distribution channel, product, and regions.

In financial management, the net present value (NPV) of a projected stream of income from a project (potential investment) divided by the investment in the project. It is used to select among competing potential investments.
An indicator of whether or not a company is generating profits at an acceptable rate. It includes such measurements as return on total assets, return on equity, and profit margin.
In project management, a coordinated set of related projects and activities that are managed together in order to obtain better control.

In project management, a network analysis technique in which each activity is assigned a pessimistic, most likely, and optimistic estimate of its duration. The critical path method is then applied using a weighted average of these times for each node. PERT computes a standard deviation of the estimate of project duration. See: critical path method (CPM), graphical evaluation and review technique (GERT), network analysis, precedence diagramming method.

The activities involved in the realization of a product or service offered to customers. Responsibilities include planning, directing, and controlling one or more projects of a new or continuing nature; initiating any acquisition processes necessary to get the project work under way; and monitoring performance. See: program manager.
A person assigned program management responsibilities for the implementation activities associated with a new or ongoing product or service offering to customers. See: program management.

An electronic device that provides manufacturing operations with the ability to manage, monitor, and rapidly control hundreds of parameters, such as temperature and pressure. They are designed to operate in industrial settings and can often automate complex processes to improve efficiency and reliability.

The practice of paying suppliers based on predefined milestones and progress. These partial payments can be made upon completion of predefined stages of work or based upon a pre-determined amount or percentage of the overall price.

An endeavor with a specific objective to be met within predetermined time and dollar limitations and that has been assigned for definition or execution. See: project manufacturing, project management.
A calendar of working and nonworking days that shows when scheduled activities can be executed. See: resource calendar.

An accounting method of assigning valuations generally used in industries where services are performed on a project basis. Each assignment is unique and costed without regard to other assignments. Examples are shipbuilding, construction projects, and public accounting firm activities. Project costing is different from process costing, in which the products to be valued are homogeneous.
The elapsed duration from project start date through the project finish date.

In project management, a set of project phases (objectives definition, requirements definition, external and internal design, construction, system test, and implementation and maintenance), whose definition is determined by the needs of those controlling the project. See: project phase.

The use of skills and knowledge in coordinating the organizing, planning, scheduling, directing, controlling, monitoring, and evaluating of prescribed activities to ensure that the stated objectives of a project are achieved. See: project.
A framework of information within the project management profession that provides a detailed level of knowledge for practitioners and academics to use in the management of projects.
In project management, the personnel assigned to a project who are directly involved in management activities.

A type of manufacturing process used for large, often unique, items or structures that require a custom design capability (engineer-to-order (ETO)). This type of process is highly flexible and can cope with a broad range of product designs and design changes. This process usually uses a fixed-position type layout. See: batch (fourth definition), continuous production, fixed-position manufacturing, job shop (second definition), process manufacturing, project, repetitive manufacturing.
A time-phased project planning and control tool that itemizes major milestones and points of user approval.
A diagram showing the technological relationships among activities in a project. See: activity-on- arrow network (AOA), activity-on-node network (AON).
In project management, a set of related project activities that usually go together to define a project deliverable. See: project life cycle.

In project management, a document that has been approved by upper management for use in executing and controlling a project. It documents assumptions, outlines tasks, facilitates communication, and documents the approved budget and schedule. A project plan may exist at a summary or a detailed level.
A process in which an organization's projects are evaluated to ensure strategic alignment with the company’s goals, and to understand the benefits and risks of a potential project. See: portfolio.
Production in which each unit or small group of units is managed by a project team created especially for that purpose.

In project management, a systematic process of controlling project risk. It includes maximizing the likelihood and effect of positive events and minimizing the likelihood and effect of negative events.
In project management, a list of activities and their planned completion dates that collectively achieve project milestones. See: work breakdown structure (WBS).
The amount and type of work that needs to be done to complete the project.
All personnel associated with a particular project, including the project sponsors, project managers, leaders of core project areas, and others assigned tasks within the project plan.
A list of team member names, roles, and contact information.
A type of layout in which the good or product is stationary, and the workers come to the site to work on it.

An inventory balance projected into the future. It is the running sum of on-hand inventory minus requirements plus scheduled receipts and planned orders. Syn.: projected available inventory. See: balance.
Syn.: projected available balance (PAB).
The current estimate of the date when an activity will be completed.

The amount of inventory planned to be physically on hand at the end of a period. This quantity may differ from the projected available balance (PAB) because units may be on hand but are not able to meet future gross requirements because they are already allocated to other uses.
The current estimate of the date when an activity will begin.
Syn.: extrapolation.
An agreement to pay a stipulated amount during an agreed time period.

One of the four Ps (product, price, place, and promotion) that constitute the set of tools used to direct the business offering to the customer. Promotion is the mechanism whereby information about the product offering is communicated to the customer. It includes public relations, advertising, sales promotions, and other tools used to persuade customers to purchase the product offering. See: four Ps.
A product that is subject to wide fluctuations in sales because it is usually sold at a reduced price or with some other sales incentive.
A carrier document indicating the person signing for delivery of a shipment with the date, time, and other related information. Syn.: delivery receipt (DR).

1) In transportation, a shipment charge that is based on the weight or volume of the shipment. 2) In intermodal transportation, a rate applied when multiple modes used to transport the shipment have significantly different cost structures. The proportional rate levels the competitive balance for carriers in high-cost modes.
An assembly designed by a manufacturer that may be serviced only with component parts supplied by the manufacturer and whose design is owned or licensed by its manufacturer.

Any financial, technical, or other information that is developed at the expense of the person or other entity submitting it and deemed to be of strategic or tactical importance to the company. It may be offered to supply chain partners on a restricted-use basis.
Syn.: safety lead time.

Additional capacity maintained at non- bottleneck resources in a process to handle random variations in performance to ensure that the bottleneck resource achieves full utilization and to limit the build-up of work in process (WIP) inventory.
In theory of constraints, the amount of inventory required relative to the protective capacity in the system to achieve a specific throughput rate at the constraint. See: limiting operation.

Wrapping or covering material that provides containment, protection, and identification of inner packaging of inventory in logistics operations. The material must be contained in such a way that will support movement and storage and will fit into the dimensions of storage space and transportation equipment.

In information systems, a set of rules for defining the format and relationships for sharing information between devices. These rules govern the transmission of data across a network and serve as the grammar of data communication languages.

1) A product model constructed for testing and evaluation to see how the product performs before releasing the product to manufacture. 2) A model consisting of all files and programs needed for a business application. See: beta release.

1) A specialized product design and development process for developing a working model of a product. See: rapid prototyping. 2) A specialized system development process for performing a determination where user needs are extracted, presented, and developed by building a working model of the system. Generally, these tools make it possible to create all files and processing programs needed for the evaluation of a business application in a matter of days or hours.
The process of identifying and purchasing the support items and determining the quantity of each support item necessary to operate and maintain a system.
Acronym for prerequisite tree.
An artificial grouping of items that facilitates planning. See: modular bill of material (BOM), phantom bill of material (BOM), planning bill of material (BOM), super bill of material (BOM).
Inventory items that are prominently displayed in large quantities in an effort to stimulate customer interest in purchasing them.
The grouping of consumers according to their behavior patterns and lifestyles. See: customer segmentation.
Acronym for package-to-order.
A blockchain that is open for anyone to join, conduct transactions, and participate in the consensus process. See: private blockchain.
A form of cloud computing available to users over the public internet that is owned and maintained by a public cloud provider. See: cloud computing, private cloud.

An encryption code used in asymmetric encryption that can be shared with anyone. It requires a corresponding secure private key for decryption and facilitates secure communication across insecure networks.
A business formed under law as a separate legal entity and for which stock is publicly traded. See: partnership, private ownership, publicly traded corporation.

The warehouse space that is rented or leased by an independent business providing a variety of services for a fee or on a contract basis. These services can include product inspection, product rating, and repackaging. These facilities are typically located near primary roads, railways, or inland waterways to facilitate rapid receiving and shipping of products. See: duty paid warehouse.
A corporation whose stock is available on a national exchange. See: public ownership.
A long-term contractual agreement between a government entity and one or more private enterprises to utilize private and public resources to perform work, build infrastructure, or provide services.

Any signal that indicates when to produce or transport items in a pull replenishment system. For example, in just-in-time (JIT) production control systems, a kanban card is used as the pull signal to replenish parts to the using operation. See: pull system.

1) In production, the production of items only as demanded for use or to replace those taken for use. See: pull signal. 2) In material control, the withdrawal of inventory as demanded by the using operations. Material is not issued until a signal comes from the downstream process or operation. 3) In distribution, a system for replenishing field warehouse inventories in which replenishment decisions are made at the field warehouse itself, not at the central warehouse or plant.
A replenishment approach that utilizes customer demand as the impetus or pull to replace and optimize inventory while also reducing total net landed cost. See: pull-through distribution.

Supply chain activities that the consumer initiates. Instead of the manufacturer pushing items to stores, consumer purchases signal the manufacturer to produce more of a given product. Effectively, the consumer is pulling products to the store. See: pull-based inventory replenishment.
A short trailer (usually 26- to 28-feet long) that is often transported in tandem with one or two other trailers.
The pooling of purchasing requirements by multiple areas in a company or even across companies.

The authorization used to formalize a purchase transaction with a supplier. A purchase order (PO) should include the name, part number, quantity, description, and price of the goods or services ordered; agreed-to terms as to payment, discounts, date of performance, and transportation; and all other agreements pertinent to the purchase and its execution by the supplier. See: discrete purchase order (PO).
A communication by a supplier to advise a purchaser that a purchase order (PO) has been received. It usually implies acceptance of the order and its terms by the supplier.

A pricing strategy in which a seller offers a customer a cheaper price as part of a promotion or in exchange for increasing order volume in a single order or cumulatively over time. See: price break, quantity discount.
The difference between the amount paid to the supplier and the purchase order (PO) cost or standard cost of that item.

The practice of analyzing the costs of the individual materials, components, and activities that make up a purchase item. This analysis is one way to review prices offered by a supplier with the purpose of understanding how the price sums up with cost elements and can assist buyers to more effectively negotiate with their suppliers.
An internal document requesting the purchasing department to purchase specified materials, goods, or services in specified quantities within a specified time. See: part requisition.
An item sourced from a supplier.
The function of and the responsibility for procuring materials, supplies, and services.
A person authorized by the company to purchase goods and services for the company.
The act of buying capacity or machine time from a supplier. A company can then schedule and use the capacity of the machine or a part of the capacity of the machine as if it were in its own plant.

The total lead time required to obtain a purchased item, which includes order preparation and release time; supplier lead time; transportation time; and receiving, inspection, and putaway time. See: lead time, supplier lead time.

The process of using evaluation metrics associated with procurement, which include the assessment of a purchasing department's performance, as well as supplier measurement. See: supplier performance evaluation.

The unit of measure used when purchasing an item. This may or may not be the same as the firm's stocking unit of measure. For example, purchasing buys steel by the ton, but it may be issued and used in square inches.

A market in which many competitors offer undifferentiated products or services within a given geographical area. Competitors are forced to accept the market price for their product. See: industry structure type.
A service that results in few or no tangible products being provided to the customer (e.g., education, snow shoveling, banking, etc.).

1) In production, the production of items at times required by a given schedule planned in advance. 2) In material control, the issuing of material according to a given schedule or the issuing of material to a job order at its start time. 3) In distribution, a system for replenishing field warehouse inventories in which replenishment decision-making is centralized, usually at the manufacturing site or central supply facility. See: pull system.

The automatic updates in selected services, such as news or weather, that occur periodically as information is sent via the internet. The source of the information pushes it onto the customer. Syn.: webcasting.
A wheeled rack structure on which palletized materials are stored and pushed up a slightly sloping ramp from which they can eventually slide down to an aisle.
The decoupling point at which a system changes from being driven by a forecast to being driven by customer demand. See: order penetration point.

Removing the material from the dock (or other location of receipt), transporting the material to a storage area, placing that material in a staging area and then moving it to a specific location, and recording the movement and identification of the location where the material has been placed.
In warehousing, the elapsed time between an item's arrival at the receiving dock and its movement to a designated storage location. Syn.: dock-to-stock time. See: inbound staging.

A process that uses lights to ensure materials are placed in the correct location during replenishment. It is also used to ensure that batch-picked items are placed into the individual shipping containers correctly during order fulfillment.
1) Acronym for present value. 2) Acronym for planned value.

A forecasting technique that enables management to review and adjust forecasts made at an aggregate level and to keep lower-level forecasts in balance. The approach combines the stability of aggregate forecasts and the application of management judgment with the need to forecast many end-items within the constraints of an aggregate forecast or sales plan. See: management estimation, planning bill of material (BOM), product group forecast.
Acronym for quality assurance.
Acronym for quality control.
Acronym for quality control circle.
Acronym for quality, cost, delivery.

A control chart for evaluating the stability of a process in terms of a quality score. The quality score is the weighted sum of the count of events of various classifications, where each classification is assigned a weight. Syns.: quality chart, quality score chart.
Acronym for quality function deployment.
Acronym for quick response.
Abbreviation for quick response manufacturing.
A supplier that has passed qualification requirements and is considered to be approved for future business but is not considered to be a first-tier supplier.
Syn.: order qualifier. See: order loser, order winner.

An approach to forecasting that is based on intuitive or judgmental evaluation. It is used generally when data is scarce, not available, or no longer relevant. Common types of qualitative techniques include personal insight, sales force estimates, panel consensus, market research, visionary forecasting, and the Delphi method. Examples include developing long-range projections and new product introductions. See: historical analogy, jury of executive opinion.

Conformance to requirements or fitness for use. Quality can be defined through five principal approaches: (1) Transcendent quality is an ideal and a condition of excellence. (2) Product-based quality is based on a product attribute. (3) User-based quality is fitness for use. (4) Manufacturing-based quality is conformance to requirements. (5) Value-based quality is the degree of excellence at an acceptable price. Also, quality has two major components: (1) quality of conformance, which is quality defined by the absence of defects, and (2) quality of design, which is quality measured by the degree of customer satisfaction with a product’s characteristics and features.
A proactive approach that establishes practices and processes to prevent quality issues from occurring instead of reacting after they have already occurred. See: quality control (QC).

A producer’s responsibility to provide 100 percent acceptable quality material to the consumer of the material. The objective is to reduce or eliminate shipping or receiving quality inspections and line stoppages as a result of supplier defects.

A systematic, independent examination and review to determine whether quality activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve the objectives.
A property of a product or service that determines the extent to which it performs and meets customer requirements and expectations.
Syn.: Q-chart.

A small group of people who normally work as a unit and meet frequently to uncover and solve problems concerning the quality of items produced, process capability, or process control. Syn.: quality control circle (QCC). See: small- group improvement activity.
The process of measuring quality conformance by comparing actual performance with a standard for the characteristic and taking corrective actions to resolve differences. See: quality assurance (QA).
Syn.: quality circle.

The overall costs associated with prevention activities and the improvement of quality throughout the firm before, during, and after production of a product. These costs fall into four recognized categories: internal failure costs, external failure costs, appraisal costs, and prevention costs. Syn.: cost of quality. See: cost of poor quality.
The engineering discipline concerned with improving the quality of products and processes.

A methodology designed to ensure that all the major requirements of the customer are identified and subsequently met or exceeded through the resulting product design process and the design and operation of the supporting production management system. QFD tries to eliminate the gap between what the customer wants in a new product and what the product is capable of delivering. QFD often leads to a clear identification of the customer’s major requirements, which are referred to as the voice of the customer (VOC). See: design for quality (DFQ), design for six sigma (DFSS), house of quality (HOQ), voice of the customer (VOC).

A parabolic approximation of the quality loss, expressed in monetary units, that occurs when a quality characteristic deviates from its target value. The cost of deviating from the target increases quadratically as the quality characteristic moves farther from the target. The formula used to compute the quality loss function depends on the type of quality characteristic being used. The quality loss function was first introduced in this form by Genichi Taguchi. See: ideal quality.
A top-management statement of the overall quality direction of an organization as required by ISO 9001.
Syn.: Q-chart.

A three-pronged approach to managing quality proposed by Joseph Juran. The three legs are quality planning (developing the products and processes required to meet customer needs), quality control (QC) (meeting product and process goals), and quality improvement (achieving unprecedented levels of performance). Syn.: Juran Trilogy.

Key interconnected factors that drive customer satisfaction. Firms must prioritize these factors and manage their trade-offs to find an equilibrium that aligns with the firm's strategy and meets customer expectations.

An approach to forecasting in which historical demand data is used to project future demand. Extrinsic and intrinsic techniques are typically used. See: extrinsic forecasting method, intrinsic forecast method.

A price reduction allowance determined by the quantity or value of a purchase. The discount could apply to all units in the order or just the marginal units in an order that exceed a given threshold. See: price break, purchase price discount.
A variation of the economic order quantity (EOQ) model in which the assumption of a single price is relaxed and there is a schedule of prices based on specific volumes. Syn.: price-break model.

The quantity of a component to be used in the production of its parent. This value is stored in the bill of material (BOM) and is used to calculate the gross requirements for components during the explosion process of material requirements planning (MRP).
Syn.: fixed order quantity (FOQ) inventory model.
The act of setting aside items from availability for use or sale until all required quality tests have been performed and conformance certified.

A type of service operation that closely resembles a manufacturing process by requiring large investments of capital and having minimal contact with customers. The focus is on standardizing the production process and increasing service reliability. Examples include postal services and fast-food operations.
In marketing, a slang term for a low-market- share but high-growth-rate product. See: growth-share matrix.
A waiting line. In manufacturing, this refers to the jobs at a given work center waiting to be processed. As queues increase, so do average queue time and work in process (WIP) inventory.
A parameter in queuing theory that specifies the order in which waiting items (e.g., products or customers) are to be served.
The quantity of items in a queue that are awaiting service.
Activities that address an excess number of items, such as products or customers, waiting in line for service.
The ratio of the actual size of a queue to the planned or scheduled queue size.

The amount of time a job waits at a work center before setup or work is performed on the job. Queue time is one element of total manufacturing lead time. Increases in queue time result in direct increases to manufacturing lead time and work-in-process inventories.
The collection of models dealing with waiting line problems, such as products or customers arriving at a service facility at which waiting lines or queues may build. Syn.: waiting line theory.
Syn.: quick ratio.

The ability to shorten machine setups between different machine operation requirements to increase process flexibility. The first priority is reducing external setup time, and the second focuses on internal setup issues. Quick changeovers reduce economic lot sizes, queue and manufacturing lead times, and work in process (WIP) inventory. It also improves quality, process, and material flows. See: single- digit setup (SDS), single-minute exchange of die (SMED).

A measure of a firm’s financial stability, which reflects its ability to meet its short-term liabilities with its most-liquid assets. It is calculated by subtracting inventory and prepaid expenses from current assets and then dividing that amount by current liabilities. A value greater than 1 is desirable and signifies that the firm has enough current assets to cover its current liabilities. Syns.: acid test, acid test ratio, quick asset ratio. See: liquidity ratio.

A supply chain system that links final retail sales with production and shipping schedules back through the chain of supply to reduce lead times and increase responsiveness. This system employs point of sale (POS) scanning and electronic data interchange (EDI) and may use direct shipment from a factory to a retailer. See: continuous replenishment, supplier-managed inventory.

A two-dimensional barcode capable of storing product information that can be used for a wide variety of activities, such as inventory management, tracking and tracing goods, differentiating authentic items from counterfeit products, and verifying warranties.

A company-wide strategy to cut lead times in all phases of manufacturing and office operations. With its roots in the time-based competition strategies, QRM focuses on the relentless pursuit of lead time reduction. While using manufacturing resources planning (MRP II) for higher-level planning, QRM often uses a replenishment technique called paired-cell overlapping loops of cards with authorization (POLCA), which combines the advantages of push and pull strategies.

A statement of price, terms of sale, and a description of goods or services offered by a supplier to a prospective purchaser. When given in response to an inquiry, it is usually considered an offer to sell. See: bid.
The date on which a quoted price is no longer valid.
A control chart in which the subgroup range, R, is used to evaluate the stability of the variability within a process. Syn.: range chart.
Abbreviation for research and development.
Syn.: experimental order. RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed)

A tool that identifies who is responsible, who is accountable, who should be consulted, and who should be kept informed for various aspects of a project or process. See: responsibility assignment matrix (RAM).

A storage device for handling material in pallets. A rack usually provides storage for pallets arranged in vertical sections with one or more pallets to a tier. Some racks accommodate more than one-pallet-deep storage. See: rack jobber.
A full-function intermediary who performs all regular warehousing functions and some retail functions, typically stocking a display rack. See: rack.

A system used to store data about items through the use of electronic tags and electromagnetic transmitters. RFID systems can be used to locate items or track material as it moves and do not require close proximity or line-of-sight access.

The spacing of the width of the rails on a railway track, measured between the inner sides of the rails. In rail transport, this is a key parameter in determining interoperability because all vehicles must have running gear that is compatible with the spacing. However, this spacing can vary among countries and cause compatibility issues.

A non-negotiable freight document that indicates that goods have been received for shipment by rail. The shipper receives a copy as a receipt for acceptance. The rail waybill contains information about the shipment such as a description of the freight, the destination address, and contact information for both the shipper and consignee.
Acronym for responsibility assignment matrix.
The speed at which a company expands or grows. Syn.: growth trajectory.
A manner of storing records in a computer file so that an individual record may be accessed without reading other records.
Syn.: common cause.
A component of demand usually describing the impact of uncontrollable variation on demand. See: time series analysis, time series decomposition.
An outcome that is not known in advance and occurs unpredictably without a distinct pattern or cause.
A machine-learning algorithm that uses the ensemble method to combine predictions from individual regression trees.

A sequence of integers or a group of numbers (often in the form of a table) whose members show absolutely no relationship to each other anywhere in the sequence. At any point, all values have an equal chance of occurring, and they occur in an unpredictable fashion.
A selection of observations taken from all the observations of a phenomenon in such a way that each chosen observation has the same possibility of selection.
A fluctuation in data or process output that is caused by uncertain or random occurrences. See: noise, random event.

A storage strategy in which parts are placed in any space that is empty when they arrive at the facility. Although this random method requires the use of a locator record to identify part locations, it often requires less storage space than a fixed-location storage method. Syns.: floating inventory location system, floating storage location. See: fixed- location storage.
In statistics, the spread in a series of observations. For example, the anticipated demand for a particular product might vary from a low of 10 items to a high of 500 items per week. The
10 or 490. See: dispersion.
Syn.: R chart.
Malicious software that renders a computer system useless by blocking access to the data until the ransom (or money) is paid.

1) The transformation of product designs into physical prototypes early in the product development process. Rapid prototyping relies on techniques such as cross- functional teams, data sharing, and advanced computer and communication technology (e.g., CAD, CAM, stereolithography, and data links). It improves product development times and allows for cheaper and faster product testing, assessment of the ease of assembly and costs, and design validation before actual production tooling. 2) The transformation of system designs into computer system prototypes with which the users can experiment to determine the adequacy of the design to address their needs. See: 3D printing.

A replenishment strategy in which the supplier prepares shipments at predetermined intervals and varies the quantity based on recent sales data. Sales data may be supplied via a point of sale (POS) system. See: continuous replenishment, supplier-managed inventory.
The primary shipping point in a local area that acts as a reference point to establish transportation rates within the area.
The total increase or decrease of an investment over a specific time period relative to the investment's initial cost. See: internal rate of return.
The gain or loss from an investment divided by the original investment cost, expressed as a percentage.
The difference between the actual output rate of product and the planned or standard output rate.

A method for scheduling and producing based on a periodic rate (e.g., daily, weekly, or monthly). This method has traditionally been applied to high-volume and process industries. The concept has also been applied within job shops using cellular layouts and mixed-model level schedules when the production rate is matched to the selling rate.

The expected output capability of a resource or system using estimates of standard performance. The rated capacity is equal to hours available × efficiency × utilization. Syns.: calculated capacity, effective capacity, nominal capacity.
The situation wherein a principal that has failed to denounce an agent’s unauthorized conduct is consequently bound by the conduct.
A process of reducing the population of elements such as stock keeping unit (SKU) counts or suppliers to reduce redundancy, increase efficiency, and improve focus.

The allocation of scarce inventory to customers when demand exceeds available supply. Rationing manages shortages by prioritizing customers based on factors such as established relationships, purchase history, customer loyalty, or stated urgency.
Purchased items or extracted materials that are converted via the manufacturing process into components and products.
The unprocessed (or minimally processed) materials held in inventory that will be used as inputs into a firm's production process.
Acronym for risk breakdown structure.
Acronym for rough-cut capacity planning.
The percentage of target customers who receive an advertising message.
Syn.: breakdown maintenance.
A special vessel used to contain a chemical reaction.
Land and associated rights improvements, utility systems, buildings, and other structures.
Up-to-date visibility resulting from the coordination of data processing with external related physical events as they occur, thereby permitting prompt reporting of conditions.
The use of a combination of technology such as GPS, barcodes, and internet of things (IoT) sensors to track the real-time movement and location of in- transit packages.
A pricing strategy that allows a company to profit but not to achieve monopolistic profits. This is normally determined by industry pricing analysis.
A return of part of the original payment for a product or service to incentivize the customer to make the purchase.

A step in the reverse logistics process when parts or products are requested to be returned because of a product defect or potential hazard resulting from government regulations or liability concerns.
1) The physical acceptance of an item into a facility or stocking location. 2) The transaction reporting the acceptance of a physical item or an order.
The average length of time required to collect payment from customers on credit sales. Syns.: average collection period, days sales outstanding (DSO).

The function encompassing the physical receipt of material, the inspection of the shipment for conformance with the purchase order (PO) (quantity and damage), the identification of and delivery to the destination within the receiving organization, and the preparation of receiving reports.

The practice of inspecting goods upon receipt for any delivery discrepancies such as damage, incorrect quantity compared with purchase order (PO) or delivery paperwork, and incomplete or incorrect paperwork.
The location to which material is being shipped. Ant.: shipping point.
A document used by the receiving function of a company to inform others of the receipt of goods purchased.
A customer classification approach that identifies customers who have purchased recently, made many purchases over time, and spent large amounts of money.
The process of changing the consignee, destination, or route of an in-transit shipment from the information contained on the bill of lading (B/L).
A collection of related data fields arranged in a predefined format that a software application treats as a unit.

A measure of the conformity of recorded values in a computer system to the actual values. An example of this is the on-hand balance of an item maintained in an electronic record relative to the actual on-hand balance of the items in the stockroom.

A reverse logistics strategy for the activities involved in the collection of used and discarded products, components, and materials. It focuses on reuse, repair, refurbishment, remanufacturing, recycling, or disposal. The objective is to recover as much of the economic value as possible, reduce waste, and minimize environmental impacts.

A period of time when capacity of a process exceeds demand to allow the system to clear previously- backlogged jobs. If there is not enough recovery time before the next episode of insufficient capacity, in-process inventory and lead times continue to grow.

A process that transforms waste material into new products but requires a significant amount of energy and resources. Recycling occupies a position in the middle of the waste hierarchy. It is not as attractive as waste reduction and reuse, but it captures higher value from waste streams than the material recovery or disposal options.

An experiment developed by W. Edwards Deming to illustrate the impossibility of putting employees in rank order of performance. The experiment shows that it would be a waste of management’s time to try to determine why one worker produced more errors than another. Management should instead improve the system, making it possible for everyone to achieve higher quality.
The lowest-level buffer zone in drum-buffer-rope scheduling where the red color is used to indicate a serious situation for the buffer.

1) A backup capability, coming either from extra machines or from extra components within a machine, to reduce the effects of breakdowns. 2) The use of one or more extra or duplicating components in a system or equipment (often to increase reliability).
A backup part of a machine or product designed to ensure uninterrupted operation.
A refrigerated cargo ship that is used to transport perishable goods requiring temperature control.

A simulation model with accurate operational details and demand forecasts that can provide practical capacity utilization predictions. Various alternatives for system operation can be evaluated effectively.
A temperature-controlled boxcar used to transport perishable goods.
Syn.: remanufactured part.

An industrial process that restores a used product to working condition only through the cleaning, repair, or replacement of essential parts and components. Refurbishing represents a less comprehensive restoration than remanufacturing.
Abbreviation for regeneration MRP. Pronounced “ree- jen.”

A material requirements planning (MRP) processing approach in which, to maintain valid priorities, the master production schedule (MPS) is totally re-exploded down through all bills of material (BOMs). New requirements and planned orders are completely recalculated or regenerated at that time. Ant.: net change MRP.

A process used to audit a company's operations with respect to a set of standard requirements to attain a registered status. The audit is conducted on site by an accredited, independent third-party organization. After a successful audit outcome, the company is certified as having met the standard requirements.

A statistical technique for determining the best mathematical expression describing the functional relationship between or among one response and one or more independent variables. See: least-squares method.
A unit that does not meet quality requirements but has not yet been sent to rework, scrapped, or returned to a supplier.
The act of identifying an item as not meeting quality specifications.

A data storage application that organizes data into tables containing rows and columns of data. The database contains logic about the relationships between the tables, which allows for effective storage and retrieval of the data to generate queries and reports.

A graphical depiction of the relationship of inputs and output flows between business functions within an organization. The map is useful to show process flows, disconnections in processes, and proposed processes.
A strategy within customer relationship management (CRM) that focuses on fostering deep, long-term connections with customers to encourage loyalty and repeat purchasing behavior.
The authorization to produce or ship material that has already been ordered.
Syn.: open order.

The time it takes from when an order is released until the beginning of the manufacturing process. This delay occurs because of the movement of materials and the changing of lines. It is non-productive time that increases lead time.

A cost incurred because of a decision. These costs would not have resulted unless the decision was made and implemented; therefore, they should be included in the analysis of decision alternatives. Ant.: sunk cost.

A bounded level of activity (such as production or sales volume) where fixed and variable cost assumptions remain valid for decision-making. Outside of this range, cost behavior may change at a different rate.

1) The probability that a product will perform its specified function under prescribed conditions without failure for a specified period of time. 2) A design parameter that can be made part of a requirements statement. 3) A Supply Chain Operations Reference Digital Standard (SCOR DS) performance attribute addressing the ability to perform tasks to meet customer requirements. Typical metrics for the reliability attribute include on time, the right quantity, and the right quality. See: mean time between failures (MTBF), mean time to failure (MTTF).

The organizational function responsible for the determination and application of appropriate reliability tasks and criteria during the design, development, manufacture, test, and support of a product that will result in the product’s reliable achievement of its specifications.
A used component or assembly that is restored to perform the original function. Syn.: refurbished part.
An industrial process that restores worn- out products to like-new, same-as-new, or better-than-new condition with respect to quality and performance. See: refurbishing.
Unscheduled maintenance performed to return a product or process to a specified performance level after a failure or malfunction.
The capability of determining the cause of a problem from an off-site location.

The practice of allowing the customer or retailer to assess the state of returned materials or products to determine if they can be reused. If an item cannot be reused, the customer or retailer can dispose of it and eliminate the costs of shipping and handling items that will ultimately be discarded. See: return material authorization (RMA).
A queuing behavior in which a service unit leaves a line after entering it but before receiving service. See: balking.
Energy that is collected from natural resources that are continually replenished, such as sunlight and wind. These are sometimes referred to as renewables.
The time period between consecutive replenishment orders.
Syn.: order point.

1) In a fixed order quantity (FOQ) inventory system, the fixed quantity that should be ordered each time the available stock (on-hand plus on-order) reaches or falls below the reorder point (ROP). 2) In a variable reorder quantity system, the quantity that should be ordered to replenish recent demand. This quantity varies from time period to time period. Syn.: replenishment order quantity.

In remanufacturing, the BOM defining the actual work required to return a product to service. The process to return a product to service is based on inspection and determination of actual requirements. See: disassembly bill of material (BOM).

The percentage of time on average that an item must be repaired for return to a serviceable condition. The repair factor is also expressed as a percentage applied to the quantity per assembly on the bill of material (BOM). It is useful for forecasting materials and capacity requirements for planning purposes. Syn.: frequency of repair. See: occurrence factor, replacement factor.
A manufacturing order detailing the work required to repair a broken, worn-out, or defective unit or piece of equipment.
A part that is used to correct a failure and to restore operational functionality to a piece of equipment. See: service part.
Syn.: service part demand.
Items that are technically feasible to repair economically.
The ability of a measurement to produce the same results when evaluating a single item or output multiple times under the same conditions.
A category of manufacturers that produces high-volume, low-variety products such as spark plugs, ball bearings, and paper clips. See: repetitive manufacturing.

The repeated production of the same discrete products or families of products. Repetitive methodology minimizes setups, inventory, and manufacturing lead times by using production lines, assembly lines, or cells. Work orders are no longer necessary; production scheduling and control are based on desired throughput rates. Products may be standard or assembled from modules. Repetitiveness is not a function of speed or volume. Syn.: repetitive process. See: discrete manufacturing, project manufacturing.
Syn.: repetitive manufacturing.
The current cost of acquiring or producing an asset, such as inventory or equipment.

The percentage of time on average that an item will require replacement. The replacement factor is also expressed as a percentage applied to the quantity per assembly on the bill of material (BOM). It is useful for forecasting materials and capacity requirements for planning purposes. See: occurrence factor, repair factor.
An order for the replacement of material that has been scrapped.

A part that can be used as a substitute but differs from completely interchangeable service parts in that it requires some physical modification (e.g., boring, cutting, or drilling) before replacing the original part.
The time it takes to implement updates into the organization’s production plan. The replan cycle occurs after completion of the last cycle and adopts a rolling horizon perspective.

In a material requirements planning (MRP) system, the amount of time between successive runs of the MRP model. If the planner does not run MRP frequently enough, the material plan becomes inaccurate because material requirements and inventory status change with the passage of time.

1) In the supply chain, the process of obtaining additional stock from a supplier. 2) Within a facility, the process of relocating material from a bulk storage area to an order pick storage area and documenting this relocation.
Syn.: replenishment period.
The total period of time that elapses from the moment it is determined that a product should be reordered until the product is back in stock and available for use.
Syn.: reorder quantity.
The time between successive replenishment orders. Syn.: replenishment interval. See: review period.
A framework that provides standards to make communications easier between web-based computer systems.
An item that has undergone selective rework or recycling.
The ability of an operation to regularly produce output of the correct quantity and quality.

To use an item for a purpose for which it was not originally intended. The item may be repaired, reconditioned, and repackaged for resale or used in a different manner through remanufacturing, recycling, or salvage.

An inquiry to a potential supplier about that supplier’s product or service for potential use in the business. The inquiry can provide certain business requirements or be of a more general exploratory nature. See: request for proposal (RFP).

A document used to solicit vendor price proposals for a particular product or service in order to compare prices. Syns.: invitation for bid (IFB), request for quote (RFQ). See: competitive bid, request for information (RFI).

A document used to solicit vendor responses when a product has been selected and price quotations are needed from several vendors. Syn.: request for proposal (RFP). See: competitive bid, invitation to tender (ITT).
Syn.: capacity required.
The specification of the inputs, files, processing, and outputs for a new system excluding any equipment alternatives and technical details.

The process of calculating the demand for the components of a parent item by multiplying the parent item requirements by the component usage quantity specified in the bill of material (BOM). Syn.: explosion.
The capability to determine the source of demand requirements through record linkages. It is used in analyzing requirements to make adjustments to plans for material or capacity. See: pegging.
Syn.: part requisition.
The ability to work around the unavailability of equipment by quickly and easily using alternate machines in the processing sequence.
The process of changing order or operation due dates, usually as a result of their being out of phase with production or customer commitments.

A fundamental assumption of material requirements planning (MRP) logic that existing open orders can be rescheduled in nearer time periods far more easily than new orders can be released and received. As a result, planned order receipts are not created until all scheduled receipts have been applied to cover gross requirements.
A message from planning system software to change the planned start and/or finish date of an order. This often is the result of a change in plans of a parent item. See: nervousness.
An organizational function that performs basic and applied research and develops potential new products.

An organization intermediate in the manufacturing and distribution process, such as a wholesaler, distributor, or retailer, that purchases goods or services with the intention of selling them rather than consuming or using them.
The process of designating stock for a specific order or schedule. See: allocation, reserve stock.
Contingency funds set aside to mitigate risk.

On-hand inventory units that have been set aside for a specific purpose, such as filling a backorder or a customer pre-order, planned use during a promotional event, or internal employee use. These units are not available for general sale to fulfill new orders even though they are currently on hand. See: allocated material, reservation.
Syns.: allocated material, assigned material.
Returning the location of production, manufacturing and service activities back to the organization's home country.
The net operating income that an investment center earns above the minimum required return on its operating assets.
Inventory created by the canceling or rescheduling of an order or left over because of lot sizing.

In the supply chain, the ability to return to a position of equilibrium after experiencing an event that causes operational results to deviate from expectations. Resilience can be improved by increasing the number of response options and/ or decreasing the time to execute those options. Resilience is improved by risk monitoring and control.

A benchmark used by publicly-traded U.S. companies in consumer electronics, retail, and pharmaceutical industries to assess supply chain resilience. The framework uses 31 indicators to determine operational and strategic supply chain resilience.
Anything that adds value to a good or service in its creation, production, or delivery.
A hierarchical structure that breaks resources into categories and types. This structure can be useful for plan resource schedules, including human resources.
A calendar of working days and nonworking days that shows when resources are idle. Typically, the calendar includes holidays and weekends and shows them as nonworking days. See: shop calendar.
Simultaneous need for a common resource. See: concurrency.

An object linked to an activity that consumes resources at a specified rate. For example, a resource driver is a purchase order (PO) (the object) that when placed (the activity) consumes hours (the rate) of purchasing (the resource).

The process of scheduling (and rescheduling) the start and finish dates of operations (or activities) to achieve a consistent rate of resource usage so that resource requirements do not exceed resource availability for a given time period.
A project schedule with no early or late start or finish dates. The activity and scheduled start and finish dates show the expected availability of resources. Syn.: resource-constrained schedule.

The effective identification, planning, scheduling, execution, and control of all organizational resources to produce a good or service that provides customer satisfaction and supports the organization’s competitive priorities and ultimately its organizational goals. Resource management emphasizes the systems perspective, encompassing both the product and process life cycles, and focusing on the integration of organizational resources toward the effective realization of organizational goals. Syn.: integrated resource management (IRM).

Capacity planning conducted at the business plan level. Resource planning is the process of establishing, measuring, and adjusting limits or levels of long-range capacity, particularly those resources that take a long time to acquire or implement. It is normally based on the production plan but may be driven by higher-level plans beyond the time horizon of the production plan (e.g., the business plan). Resource planning decisions always require top management approval. Syn.: resource requirements planning. See: capacity planning, long-term planning.

The standard hours of load placed on a resource by time period. Production lead-time data is taken into account to provide time-phased projections of the capacity requirements for individual production facilities. See: bill of resources, capacity planning using overall factors (CPOF), product load profile, rough-cut capacity planning (RCCP).
Syn.: resource planning.
Syn.: resource limited schedule.

The practice of scheduling activities so that predetermined resource availability pools are not exceeded. Activities are started as soon as resources are available (with respect to logical constraints), as required by the activity. When not enough of a resource exists to accommodate all activities scheduled on a given day, a priority decision is made. Project completion may be delayed, if necessary, to alter schedules constrained by resource usage.
The elapse of time or average delay between the initiation of a transaction and the results of the transaction.
A tool to ensure that each component of work in a project is assigned to a responsible person. See: RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed) chart.
A landfill operation designed to turn waste into recoverable resources, minimize the amount of space consumed, and maximize the operational life of the landfill.

The practice of ensuring the use of ethical sources of goods and services where a firm does business to bring about a positive impact and minimize the negative impacts on societies and environments. This includes processes for identifying, assessing, and managing the environmental, social, and ethical risks in the supply chain. Another important strategy is reducing, reusing and recycling materials. Syn.: environmentally responsible purchasing.

The ability to sense demand exceptions; target revenue opportunities; and resolve supply challenges through planning of constrained resources (material, labor, and equipment capacity) and the allocation of supply across the network to best meet demand aligned with the business strategy.

The speed or promptness with which an organization or supply chain provides products and services to the customer. Responsiveness is a performance attribute within the resilience performance category in the Supply Chain Operations Reference Digital Standard (SCOR DS) model.
Acronym for representation state transfer.
The unit or aggregate value realized from not disposing of a return but instead renewing it for future use.
To use a system backup to recover lost data and transactions after a data loss event. See: backup.

A method of inventory valuation in which the value of an organization's cost of goods sold (COGS) is determined by applying the cost-to-sales ratio (i.e., cost divided by retail price) to the total sales revenue over a specified time period. This method assumes that the historical markup used to compute the cost-to-sales ratio remains constant for all products in the current period.
A business that takes title to products and resells them to final consumers.
A percentage of a contract value that is withheld pending project completion and approval.
In marketing, a measurement of how well a company maintains repeat customers.
The termination of a debt obligation by appropriate settlement with the lender. Repayment or forgiveness is understood to be in full amount unless partial settlement is specified.
A modification made to in-service equipment or an existing facility to enhance its performance, capacity, or function.

The activities associated with the reverse flow of goods and services. Detailed activities encompass identification of the need to return, disposition decision-making, scheduling of the return, and shipment and receipt of the returned goods. In the Supply Chain Operations Reference Digital Standard (SCOR DS), this also includes any service components from a customer in order to diagnose condition and evaluate entitlement.
A measure of an organization's ability to quickly adapt its strategic and operational return process capabilities in response to changes in return requirements.

A document that provides information about why a part or product is being returned and provides a decision to the customer on whether a return is authorized. This enables the supplying company to plan for the next appropriate action or actions, such as shipping a replacement unit to the customer, scheduling the return unit for warranty repair, scheduling the return unit for a repair not covered by warranty, returning the unit to stock, or returning the unit to the vendor. See: return material authorization (RMA).
A status in which the customer must request and receive permission from a supplier to return a product for a replacement, exchange, or refund. See: return material authorization (RMA).
The process of recovering part or all of the cost from the vendor when a defect in a returned item is determined to be related to a component purchased from that vendor.
The average time associated with return processes, which typically start with the decision to return a product and end with collecting and restocking the product.
A cost that occurs from discarding or recycling products that are returned because of defects, customer rejection, obsolescence, or end of life.
The work a company puts into processing returned goods from its customers.
Combining customer deliveries with pickups for returned items to optimize transportation efficiency. See: backhauling.

1) A form that must be completed that describes the product returned and why it was returned. Syn.: return merchandise authorization. See: return authorization. 2) A number given to authorize the acceptance of returned items. See: pre-issued return authorization, remote return authorization. 3) The signatory authorization that is normally required to return the goods. See: return authorization required.
Syn.: return material authorization (RMA).

A relative measure of financial performance that describes the extent to which an organization has used its assets to create profit. ROA is computed as net income over a specified time period (such as a year) divided by total assets. See: return on net assets (RONA), return on owner’s equity (ROE).

A relative measure of financial performance that provides a means for comparing various investments by computing the ratio of the net profit earned during a specified time period to the cost of the investment. In theory of constraints (TOC), the net profit used in the ROI calculation is the difference between throughput and operating expenses.
The ratio of a company’s profit to its fixed net assets. See: return on assets (ROA).

A financial measurement of how successful a company is in creating income for the owners of the organization. A comparison of the ROE with the return on assets (ROA) indicates the effectiveness of financial leverage employed by the firm. The measurement is calculated by dividing net income by average owner’s equity. See: return on assets (ROA).

word: return on supply chain fixed assets
definition: A measurement of the return an organization receives from its invested capital in supply chain fixed assets. This includes the fixed assets used in Orchestrate, Plan, Order, Source, Transform, Fulfill, and Return. It is calculated as (Supply Chain Revenue – Total Supply Chain Management Cost) ÷ Supply Chain Fixed Assets.
A measure of profit on the amount of capital consumed. It is calculated as after-tax operating income divided by net working capital.

The options for a returned product that will be transformed and placed back into stock or sent directly to a customer. These options include reuse, recycle, remanufacture, refurbish, upcycle, downcycle, etc., for reverse supply chains, return supply chains, and replenish supply chains.

Providing returned goods to alternate channels for resale into the market. The resale may include refurbished goods, where the secondary channel may be responsible for product support and warranty on refurbished products.
Financial protection from problems that might occur with high-value excess inventory return shipments.
The routing of authorized returns to central hubs or facilities where they can be combined and routed to the correct location in order to eliminate the need for sorting.
Material that was rejected by the buyer’s inspection department and is awaiting shipment back to the supplier for repair or replacement.
Following the path of a return shipment by using the tracking number assigned by the carrier.
Product sent back from a customer because of being defective, damaged, out of season, an incorrect shipment, outdated (end-of-life), excess inventory, or no longer wanted.
The quantity of product that a customer is allowed to return, usually calculated as a percentage of total purchases. This quantity may be captured in a contract or warranty.
A facility where an organization's returns are processed. This is also commonly referred to as a centralized return center.

The review process for returned goods generally performed at the point of return. Dispositioning options may include: repair and return to user, return to stock, repair and refurbish, resell, or send to salvage. Each of these options may involve different service providers and practices.
A process of handling returns that includes environmentally sound disposal or recycling, composition of repair instructions, warranty repairs, and collection of return data.

A software solution for managing the returns process, including the tracking of return authorizations, receiving and processing of returned goods, shipping, quality assurance (QA), metrics, and other reporting.
All of the costs associated with dealing with returned items after they have been received. These costs occur when returned items are repaired, discarded, or replaced.

One of the elements of the waste hierarchy that focuses on the use of an item for a new or similar purpose with only minimal reprocessing. Reuse differs from remanufacture as it assumes less repair or reclamation activity to the reused good.

The income received by a company from sales of products or services. Revenues can come from other sources including stock owned in other companies, income from selling property, or other company assets that are not a typical part of the core business.
An internet auction in which suppliers bid to sell products or services at a lower cost than competitors.

The process of disassembling, evaluating, and redesigning a competitor’s product for the purpose of manufacturing a product with similar characteristics without violating any of the competitor’s proprietary manufacturing technologies.

A scheduling procedure used in some process industries for building process train schedules. The scheduling starts with the last stage and proceeds backward through the process structure. See: process flow scheduling.
A complete supply chain dedicated to the reverse flow of products and materials for the purpose of returns, repair, remanufacture, and/or recycling.
A third-party service that arranges for the processing and disposal of returned products. See: third- party logistics (3PL).

In the Supply Chain Operations Reference Digital Standard (SCOR DS), the practice of checking the amount of leftover raw material after each item is produced and returning the leftover raw material to inventory to maintain an accurate raw material inventory count. This practice is most useful in production environments in which the required amount of raw materials tends to vary between units. See: backflush.
The planning and controlling of the processes of moving goods from the point of consumption back to the point of origin for repair, reclamation, recycling, or disposal. See: reverse logistics.
The time between successive evaluations of inventory status to determine whether to reorder. See: fixed order interval inventory model, replenishment period.
A number or letter representing the number of times a part drawing or specification has been changed.
The reprocessing of a defective product or service to restore it to acceptable quality or to salvage it.
The time required to rework material in-house or at a supplier’s location.
A manufacturing order to rework and salvage defective parts or products.
Acronym for radio frequency identification.
Acronym for recency, frequency, monetary.
Acronym for request for proposal.
Acronym for request for quote.
Acronym for right first time.

A six sigma quality principle that refers to the concept that it is beneficial and more cost-effective to take the necessary steps the first time to ensure that a good or service meets its requirements than to provide a good or service that will need rework or not meet customers’ needs. In other words, an organization should engage in defect prevention rather than defect detection.

word: right size frequency of production wheel
definition: A lean scheduling tool used to produce standard production sequences for different items in a high-product-mix environment to minimize changeovers and increase throughput. See: mixed-model scheduling.
A United States labor policy that allows workers to choose whether or not to join a union.

A decision to take no action to deal with a risk rather than mitigate or avoid it. This is often because of the cost of managing the risk being less than the cost or benefit of mitigating the risk. See: risk avoidance, risk management, risk mitigation, risk tolerance.
A financial metric that compares risk with return by including the level of project risk in the calculation of the valuation.
The amount and type of risk that an organization is willing to pursue or retain.
An activity in risk management that determines the impact and probability of a risk.
Changing a plan to eliminate a risk or to protect plan objectives from its impact. See: risk acceptance, risk management.
