The act of placing customer-requested stickers on the boxes of the product being shipped to them. The typical purpose is to enable the customer, usually a retailer, to track its inventory more effectively. See: barcoding.
A model that explicitly considers the effect of uncertainty within the analysis.

1) A quantity of items held in inventory. 2) Stored products or service parts ready for sale. These are distinct from a store, which usually consists of components or raw materials. 3) An investment security that represents partial ownership of a firm's assets and earnings.
Syn.: item number.

A unique code that is used by warehouses, distribution centers (DCs), and retailers to identify and track inventory at a particular location. One product stocked at various locations may be represented by unique SKUs at each location.
Syn.: item rationalization.
Syn.: item number.
An order to replenish on-hand stock, as opposed to a production order to make a particular product for a specific customer.
Inventory information for a given item including the quantities ordered, received, issued, and returned, enabling the firm to track the on-hand balance of the item.
A report showing the inventory on hand and often the inventory on order and sales or usage history for a specific product.
Syn.: expedite.

The smallest unit of measure for an item in an inventory management system. It is used to determine the value of inventory and is the basis for converting quantities to the purchasing unit of measure.
Syn.: just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing.

1) The purchase of materials, parts, and supplies for direct delivery to departments or manufacturing workstations instead of receiving them into and issuing them from warehouse storage. See: dock-to-stock inventory. 2) A procurement strategy in which buyers negotiate prices for required annual volumes of items up front but the supplier holds the inventory until the buyers place individual orders for the items as they are needed. See: blanket purchase order (PO), blanket release.
A lack of materials, components, or finished goods that are needed to meet demand. See: backorder.
A signal or notification of an item indicating a lack of inventory on hand that is required.
A cost associated with a stockout occurrence, which may include lost sales, backorder costs, expediting, and additional manufacturing and purchasing costs.

A measure of the effectiveness with which a company responds to actual demand or requirements. The stockout percentage can be a comparison of total orders containing a stockout with total orders or of line items incurring stockouts with total line items ordered during a period. One formula is stockout percentage = (1 – customer service ratio) × 100 percent. Ant.: customer service ratio.
The likelihood of a product not being in stock when an order is placed. See: cycle service level.

A designated location in an active area of operation into which material is placed and from which it is taken. This represents a way of tracking and controlling active material. The stockpoint is not necessarily a stockroom isolated from activity.

A method of loading freight in which the items are loaded onto a trailer in reverse order of their delivery, with the last items to be delivered being loaded first and the first items to be delivered being loaded last.
Syn.: hold order.
The retention of parts or products for future use or shipment.
A subset of inventory carrying costs, including the cost of warehouse rent and utilities, material handling personnel, equipment maintenance, insurance, building maintenance, and security personnel.
1) Inventory of raw materials used in making a product. 2) A storage point located upstream of a workstation where raw materials, components, assemblies, and tools are kept.
A card on which records of the items on hand and on order are maintained.
Syn.: picking list.

A technique based on the plan-do-check-action (PDCA) problem-solving process, which is a visual method of breaking down complex problems into smaller pieces and determining the steps needed to resolve the problem.

The degree to which an item affects space utilization of a trailer or container during transport. It considers physical item characteristics such as excessive weight, irregular shape, or the ability to be stacked. Stowability is one factor used in determining shipment costs and classifying freight. Items that result in empty space in the trailer or container will generally be charged a higher rate.

A method for loading pallets in which the longest side of the pallet is parallel to the side of the trailer, container, or railcar. Straight loading is generally the fastest method of loading and can facilitate the loading of multiple pallets at the same time.
A method of depreciation whereby the value of a long-term asset is reduced uniformly in equal annual installments over its estimated useful life.
Syn.: gapped schedule.
The development of supply chain partners with a commitment to the shared purpose and objectives focused on accomplishing a coordinated supply chain strategy.

A relationship formed by two or more organizations that share proprietary information, participate in joint investments, and develop linked and common processes to increase the performance of both companies. Many organizations form strategic alliances to increase the performance of their common supply chain.
Evaluation of the way in which other organizations, often in different industries, compete.
A division of a large organization that operates like a separate organization with its own vision, mission, and goals and offers specific products or services in a market segment.
A long-range plan that has a significant effect on how the organization accomplishes its mission and business strategy.
Syn.: hoshin planning.

Continuously researching and analyzing the various available options for a particular process, and then selecting the most relevant option that aligns with the organization's strategic goals. See: strategic plan.
A factor that influences the way an organization plans to achieve its goals. See: strategic variable.

The process of determining the location of inventory in the production process or the supply chain that will protect against variability, decouple lead times, and enable responsiveness to changes in demand.

A statement of the future business scope of an enterprise. It incorporates what is being satisfied (customer needs), who is being satisfied (customer groups), and how the company creates value for the customer (processes, technologies, and core competencies).
A formal arrangement with a major supplier or customer to work together and share information and resources to improve supply chain performance.

A measurement that relates to the long-term goals of a business. Examples include profitability, market share, growth, and productivity. See: global measurements, operational performance measurement, performance objective.
A plan that describes the specific actions necessary to support and accomplish the mission, goals, and objectives of an organization. See: business plan, strategic planning, strategy, tactical plan.
The process of developing a strategic plan. See: operational plan, operational planning, strategic plan, tactical planning.
The process of including quality considerations and objectives into a strategic plan.

A comprehensive approach for locating and sourcing key material suppliers, which often includes the business process of analyzing total-spend-for-material spend categories. The approach includes a focus on the development of long-term relationships with trading partners who can help the purchaser meet profitability and customer satisfaction goals.

An important factor that affects the organization's ability to achieve its strategic goals. Examples typically include the economic situation, population demographics, changes in technology, and government policies. See: strategic driver.

A plan that defines how a company will function in its environment. The strategy specifies how to satisfy customers, how to grow the business, how to compete in its environment, how to manage the organization and develop capabilities within the business, and how to achieve financial objectives. See: strategic plan.

A statistical tool for determining root causes in which observed historical data is separated by particular characteristics to determine the effect of each characteristic upon the observed results. See: root cause analysis.
A system of interconnecting lines and points representing streets and roads for a specified area. It is used to find the best routes or to create a specified service area.
The requirement that a party must fulfill its obligations exactly as stated in the contract without any deviation to warrant payment.

A defined process applied to determine, evaluate, and resolve an identified problem. The methodology includes (1) collecting factual data, (2) defining why the situation is a problem, (3) composing a concise definition of what the problem is, (4) generating possible solutions, (5) evaluating the pros and cons of each option within the organization’s objectives and feasibility, and (6) implementing the solution selected.
A part that is assembled separately and is used as an input at the next level of the bill of material (BOM) in the production of a larger unit.
Sending production or service work outside to another manufacturer. See: outsourcing.

A solution to a problem that is best from a narrow point of view but not from a higher or overall company point of view. For example, a department manager who refuses to allow employees to work overtime in order to minimize the department’s operating expense may cause lost sales and a reduction in overall company profitability.
An organizational structure within a factory consisting of a compact entrepreneurial unit that is either process-oriented or product-oriented and is structured to achieve maximum productivity.

The market condition in which a buyer is willing and able to purchase similar products from different suppliers to meet its needs. This increases the buyer’s power because the buyer doesn't have to rely on just one supplier.
The use of a similar part or component in place of a primary item, often due to lack of availability.
A supplier who delivers a product to a first-tier supplier of the customer.
In project management, an activity that can only occur after one or more predecessor activities are completed. See: activity-on-arrow network (AOA), activity-on- node network (AON).
For any collection of data points, this is the total sum of the difference between each point in the data and the average of all the data points. Syn.: cumulative forecast error (CFE).

A form of multilevel bill of material (BOM) that lists all the parts and their quantities required in a given product structure. Unlike the indented bill of material (BOM), it does not list the levels of manufacture and lists a component only once for the total quantity used.

A form of an indented where-used bill of material (BOM) that shows all parents in which a given component is used, the required quantities, and all the next- level parents until the end-item is reached. Unlike the indented where-used, it does not list the levels of manufacture.
1) A cost that has already been paid; thus, it is not relevant to a decision being made about the future. Ant.: relevant cost. 2) Capital already invested that cannot be retrieved.

A type of planning bill, located at the top level in the structure, that ties together various modular bills (and possibly a common parts bill of material (BOM)) to define an entire product or product family. The quantity per relationship of the super bill to its modules represents the forecasted percentage of demand of each module. The master-scheduled quantities of the super bill explode to create requirements for the modules that also are master scheduled. See: dynamic bill of material (BOM), pseudo bill of material (BOM).
A technique to relieve all components down to the lowest level using the complete bill of material (BOM), based on the count of finished units produced or transferred to finished goods inventory.

A storage area maintained as a buffer between stages of a production process to manage the flow of materials, parts, and components through the process. Items are stored on shelves just like a grocery store to improve picking efficiency and are restocked to ensure consistent access as they are required.
An estimate, made by a knowledgeable manager, of the labor required for an operation.
An architecture made up of computers and other devices and software that gathers data in real time from remote locations in order to control industrial processes, equipment, and conditions.
A provider of goods or services to another company. Syn.: outside shop. See: vendor.

A collaborative forum for the exchange of ideas by a company with its primary suppliers. The objective of the group, often called a supplier advisory council, is to share ways that products or services can be improved, costs can be reduced, or that customer satisfaction can be increased.

The practice of identifying suitable suppliers who can meet the planned requirements. Identification methods include conducting evaluation and appraisal questionnaires, desktop research, field research, supplier visits, supplier reference checks, and asking suppliers to complete a request for information to answer questions.
The formal evaluation of a supplier's processes, systems, and performance compared with defined requirements or standards.
The group of suppliers from which a firm acquires goods and services. Syn.: supply base.

The process of verifying that a supplier operates, maintains, improves, and documents effective procedures that relate to the customer’s requirements. Such requirements can include cost, quality, delivery, flexibility, maintenance, safety, and ISO standards related to quality and environmental management.

1) The strategic practice of grouping suppliers based on similar characteristics related to criticality, service performance, relationship type, risk exposure, and sustainability impact. See: supplier segmentation. 2) Deliberately sourcing from remote suppliers within a small geographical area to facilitate freight consolidation of what would otherwise be less-than-truckload (LTL) quantities.

A structured and effective relationship between buyers and suppliers that provides real-time visibility into transactions (including orders, invoices and credit memos) and monitors performance metrics to reduce risks, improve performance against contract terms, and achieve negotiated savings. Syn.: collaborative supply relationship. See: supplier partnership.

The practice of researching a supplier’s financial stability to understand the supplier's risk of bankruptcy or financial insolvency. This can be accomplished through a business credit check with a credit-rating agency as well as through information gathered from the supplier’s financial statements and external references.

The practice of informing suppliers about the status of the tender awarding, whether the supplier is successful or not. These debriefings assure the procurement process is transparent and equitable and permits unsuccessful suppliers an opportunity to understand why their bid was not successful.
Technical and financial assistance given to existing and potential suppliers to improve quality and/or due date performance.

A comprehensive description of the supply base for a particular material, component, or service that summarizes suppliers' geographic locations; capabilities; and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) impact. Analyzing the supplier footprint can help a firm improve its operational performance, resilience, and alignment with strategic priorities.
The amount of time that typically elapses between the time an order is received by a supplier and the time the customer receives the items. Syn.: vendor lead time. See: purchasing lead time.

Data that includes all relevant information about suppliers, including names, addresses, procurement history, supply categories, contract records, service commitments, and other key information about the supplier-business relationship. It may also include discounts, freight and delivery terms, currencies, payment terms, tolerances, and invoicing options for each supplier.
The act of measuring a supplier’s performance relative to contracted terms. Measurements often encompass delivery reliability, lead time, and price. See: vendor measurement.
A numerical code used to distinguish one supplier from another.
A supplier organization with which a company has formed a customer-supplier partnership. See: outpartnering.

A working relationship with a supplier organization whereby two organizations collaborate by sharing information and developing joint plans and strategies to meet the goals and objectives of both parties. Syn.: collaborative supply relationship. See: supplier collaboration.

The practice of monitoring and evaluating key suppliers on their cost, quality, engineering, delivery, etc., performance based on an agreed set of measurements. Syn.: supplier performance management. See: purchasing performance measurement.

The process of evaluating, monitoring, and managing a supplier’s performance based on mutually defined criteria, such as reducing costs, on-time delivery, and managing risks. Syn.: supplier performance evaluation.

The confidence that a supplier’s goods or services will fulfill its customers’ needs. This confidence is achieved by creating a relationship between the customer and supplier that ensures that the product will be fit for use with minimal corrective action and inspection.

The process of officially logging a supplier as a service or product provider in a company’s system after completing a verification process. The verification process can vary from a simple procedure of assuring that the supplier has a letter of incorporation and is licensed and registered to do business to a more complicated verification process requiring the prequalification of the supplier against a set of standards. The process systematically assures that suppliers can be issued a purchase order (PO) and that their payment can be processed through the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system and payment portals.

A comprehensive approach to managing an enterprise’s interactions with the organizations that supply the goods and services the enterprise uses. The goal of SRM is to streamline and make more effective the processes between an enterprise and its suppliers. SRM is often associated with automating procure-to-pay business processes, evaluating supplier performance, and exchanging information with suppliers.

An enterprise software system used to implement and manage supplier relationships, including the management of supplier-related data, such as purchases, supply contracts, and delivery dates. See: supplier relationship management (SRM).

A person whose main job is working with suppliers regarding what is needed and when. This person is in direct contact with both material requirements planning (MRP) and the suppliers and is responsible for material planning for the items under their control, communicating the resultant schedules to their assigned suppliers, doing follow-up to monitor status, resolving problems, and advising other planners and the master scheduler when purchased items will not arrive on time to support the schedule. Syns.: planner/buyer, vendor scheduler.

A purchasing approach that provides suppliers with schedules rather than with individual purchase orders (POs). A supplier scheduling system will often include a business agreement (contract) for each supplier, a schedule for each supplier extending for some time into the future, and a formal priority planning system that provides the supplier with valid due dates. Syn.: vendor scheduling.

A practice that organizes the relationship with suppliers by positioning them into different segments based on many parameters including transactional, preferred, strategic, or ownership relationship. Supplier segments range across a spectrum of buyer-supplier relationships such as traditional transactional suppliers, preferred suppliers, or strategic relationship suppliers. See: supplier clustering.

A high-level process map that shows substantial subprocesses in an organization’s process together with the structure of the process represented by the suppliers, inputs, outputs, and customers. A SIPOC diagram defines the critical aspects of a process without losing the overall perspective. See: process flow diagram.

A collaborative relationship in which the supplier monitors and manages inventory levels at the customer's location using data and plans that the customer shares with the supplier. See: continuous replenishment, quick response (QR), rapid replenishment, vendor-managed inventory (VMI).
An inventory system in which the supplier maintains ownership of the inventory at the customer’s location until the item is used or sold. See: consignment.

Materials used generally in manufacturing that are not normally charged to any one finished production. Examples include cutting and lubricating oils, machine repair parts, glue, or tape. Syn.: indirect materials. See: maintenance, repair, and operating (MRO) supplies.

1) The quantity of goods available for use. 2) The actual or planned replenishment of a product or component. The replenishment quantities are created in response to a demand for the product or component or in anticipation of such a demand.
Syn.: supplier base.

The strategic practice of analyzing and adjusting the number of suppliers an organization uses to effectively balance spend volumes, relationship intensity, and supply risk. Syn.: supply base rightsizing.
Syn.: supply base rationalization.
The flow of products, information and money through a network of partners from raw material suppliers to end users.
The tools and analytical processes used to combine data from multiple systems and develop insights to improve supply chain processes and performance.

An organization’s strategic and tactical capability to plan for and respond to conditions, situations, and events as necessary in order to continue supply chain operations at an acceptable predefined level.

A centralized hub that provides an integrated, complete view of data across the end-to-end supply chain. The system allows the supplier to see the requirements and inventory levels at the customer's site, enhances the ability to get accurate information about supply location and availability, and highlights any potential excess inventory. Similarly, it helps the customer easily identify supply and demand variations and take necessary actions to return excess inventory. See: digital twin.
The time it would take to fill a customer order if inventory levels were zero. It is the sum of the longest lead times for each stage in the supply chain. See: cycle service level, cycle time.

The determination of the structure of a supply chain, including the selection of partners, the location and capacity of warehouse and production facilities, the products, the modes of transportation, and supporting information systems. See: supply chain network.

A graph depicting the trade-off between supply chain cost and performance for efficient supply chains, which is useful in evaluating the efficiency of a current supply chain design and informing changes to make the current design more efficient.

A software application that provides users with the ability to flag the occurrence of certain supply chain events to trigger some form of alert or action within another supply chain application. SCEM can be deployed to monitor supply chain business processes such as planning, transportation, logistics, or procurement. It can also be applied to supply chain business intelligence applications to alert users to any unplanned or unexpected events. See: performance and event management system.

The set of processes and software applications that manage and control the use of supply chain assets to satisfy customer delivery requirements while controlling costs. This includes manufacturing, warehousing, and transportation execution systems as well as systems that provide visibility across the supply chain.
A technology-based set of processes that link the buyer, seller, and financing institution to lower financing costs and improve business efficiency.
Those fixed assets associated with the costs to Orchestrate, Plan, Order, Source, Transform, Fulfill, and Return within the supply chain.
The connection and coordination of strategy, planning, and decision-making between supply chain partners to increase mutual benefit.

The ability to digitally track and monitor the status and position of items as they move through the global supply chain. It also notifies the user of significant deviations from plans. See: supply chain visibility.

The design, planning, execution, control, and monitoring of supply chain activities with the objective of creating net value, building a competitive infrastructure, leveraging worldwide logistics, synchronizing supply with demand, and measuring performance globally.

An enterprise software system that enables a company to manage the flow of goods from the raw material state to a finished product and shipment to end users. The SCM system aligns with the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system by providing additional functionality in the areas of warehouse management, advanced planning, and transportation management.

The identification of relationships between multiple layers of upstream and downstream supply chain participants to establish total visibility of the flow of materials, products, and information through the entire supply chain.

A firm’s ability to achieve superior results through exceptional management of revenue generation, segmented supplier and customer management, collaboration and information sharing, risk management, data analysis, and appropriate use of technology.

An interconnected system of independent suppliers, manufacturers, retailers, and logistics providers that work together to enable the production and distribution of goods to satisfy customer requirements. The network structure includes the interactions and interdependencies between the companies that are required to achieve overall objectives. See: supply chain design.
A tool or application that aligns all supply chain members' goals and processes to promote the accomplishment of overall supply chain objectives.

A process reference model developed by the Supply Chain Council and endorsed by the Association for Supply Chain Management (ASCM) as the standard cross-industry diagnostic tool for supply chain management (SCM). The SCOR model describes the business activities associated with satisfying a customer’s demand, which include Orchestrate, Plan, Source, Order, Transform, Fulfill, and Return. Use of the model includes analyzing the current state of a company’s processes and goals, quantifying operational performance, and comparing company performance to benchmark data. SCOR has developed a set of metrics for supply chain performance, and ASCM members have formed industry groups to collect best practices information that companies can use to evaluate their supply chain performance. Supply Chain Operations Reference Digital Standard (SCOR

A model that provides methodology, diagnostic, and benchmarking tools that help organizations make dramatic and rapid improvements in supply chain processes. SCOR DS is a part of the ASCM body of knowledge used to foster the advancement of end-to-end supply chain management (SCM).
The use of advanced analytical tools such as simulation, digital twins, and machine learning to develop and implement strategies to improve efficiency and performance in a supply chain.

The determination of a set of policies, procedures, and parameters that govern the operation of a supply chain. Planning includes the determination of marketing channels, promotions, respective quantities and timing, inventory and replenishment policies, and production policies.
The ability of a supply chain to anticipate, create plans to avoid or mitigate, and/or to recover from disruptions to supply chain functionality. See: resilience.
Operating revenue generated from a supply chain, excluding non-operating revenue, such as leased real estate, investments, court settlements, or sales of office buildings.

The variety of possible events and their outcomes that could have a negative effect on the flow of goods, services, funds, or information resulting in some level of quantitative or qualitative loss for the supply chain.

An analysis that determines where the greatest supply chain risks may exist in order to help company leaders prioritize resources for risk mitigation and management. Assessments involve clarifying the nature of a risk, understanding conditions that may lead to the event, knowing how frequently such events have happened or can be expected to happen, and the potential impact of such events.
The systematic identification, assessment, and mitigation of potential supply chain disruptions with the objective of reducing their negative impacts on the supply chain’s performance.
A formal process to continuously observing the conditions related to a risk event to identify an increase in the probability of occurrence or impact.

The development and operation of distinct end-to-end supply chains that are optimized for the needs of each customer channel by considering product characteristics, supply capabilities, and overall business value.

An overarching plan for the design, planning, execution, control, and monitoring of supply chain activities. It is intended to guide efficient operations and initiatives that deliver on the desired key performance indicators and objectives. A supply chain strategy also specifies the function that is generally responsible for each supply chain activity as well as when collaboration among teams is needed, what needs to happen and when, and how performance will be measured.

The practice of testing the resilience of a supply chain model or strategy by evaluating and quantifying the way the supply chain behaves as the result of the occurrence of a disruption. The firm can evaluate the impact of potential risk-mitigation strategies to develop appropriate plans if such a disruption were actually to occur. See: risk response planning.

The open sharing of information to external stakeholders across the supply chain about how a product is sourced, produced, and delivered. It is used to build trust by verifying the path a product takes from raw material to consumer.

The ability to track the location and flow of materials, components, finished goods, and information throughout the supply chain in real time to improve resilience, increase customer service, and enhance supply chain relationships. See: supply chain inventory visibility, traceability.

The collection of data and information about current market dynamics and trends that can be used to develop an effective procurement strategy that can increase the value the firm realizes from its sourcing processes, improved supply risk management, and enhanced supplier relationships.

The development and rationalization of a supply network to satisfy the required service level at the lowest total landed cost. This includes managing medium- and long-term capacity decisions based on strategic initiatives and financial plans while maintaining an agile supply network.

The analysis and implementation of comprehensive tactical planning and sourcing decisions based on a single, globally consistent model. The practice enables firms to match between supply and demand by integrating purchasing, manufacturing, distribution, and transportation into one consistent model.
Adjusting the timing of the application of a demand adjustment factor to account for fluctuations in demand or long lead time components. See: demand adjustment factor (DAF).
Production rate, or quantity of units per unit of time, sent to inventory.
The risk of interruptions in the flow of materials, components, or supplies from upstream suppliers.
In activity-based cost accounting, an activity cost not directly related to producing a product, such as the cost of the information system.
An essential activity such as accounting and information systems that does not directly participate in production.
Syn.: upcharge.

An independent federal agency in the United States that oversees economic regulation of the modes of surface transportation, primarily rail carriers. The STB does, however, regulate some aspects of motor carrier pricing related to the movement of household goods.
The ability to meet sudden, unexpected increases in demand by expanding production with existing personnel and equipment.

A container to hold output from one process and feed it to a subsequent process. It is used when line balancing is not possible or practical or only on a contingency basis when downstream equipment is nonoperational.
A situation in which an oversupply exists.
In activity-based cost accounting, a substitute for the best possible driver that is useful because it is less costly and almost as accurate.
A form of research in which data is collected by distributing questionnaires to a group of people within a target audience. See: marketing research.
An organizational focus on activities that provide present benefit without compromising the needs of future generations. See: sustainable specification.

A process whereby organizations meet their needs for goods and services in a way that achieves value for the organization as well as society and the economy while minimizing damage to the environment.

The practice of specifying and documenting the business requirements for supply using sustainable standards. These specifications are developed to clearly define the ethical and environmental business requirements and effectively communicate these to suppliers to facilitate the evaluation of goods and services against the agreed specification. See: sustainability.
The management of supply chain activities to make them more environmentally friendly and socially responsible. See: green supply chain.
In activity-based cost accounting, an activity that is not directly beneficial to any specific cost object but does benefit the organization as a whole.
Acronym for schedule variance.
A type of freight container that can be interchangeably transported by either road or rail.

A framework used in risk management to characterize and mitigate risks in complicated environments such as supply chains. The Swiss Cheese Model views system failures as holes in a piece of cheese, and preventative measures and barriers against the risks as slices of cheese that limit the hole from going all the way through the piece of cheese and resulting in a total system failure such as a personal accident within a facility, a transportation accident, or a supply chain disruption.
Acronym for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
An analysis of the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of and to an organization. SWOT analysis is useful in developing strategy. See: environmental scanning.
A computer network attack where multiple identities are created in order to attack the system's reputation.

An alert in demand-driven material requirements planning (DDMRP) that highlights potential problems before they occur through expediting, rescheduling for components to coincide with parent item planned receipt, or adjusting item lead times.

The capability that enables a business’s strategy via planning and operational levers across the entire value network. This capability integrates strategic goals, financial objectives, and tactical supply network plans to create a connected, concurrent, and synchronized business plan. The result is faster cross-functional decision-making, better information visibility, enhanced customer service, an agile supply network, real-time collaboration with business partners, efficient resource usage, and improved financial performance.

A manufacturing management philosophy that includes a consistent set of principles, procedures, and techniques in which every action is evaluated in terms of the overall objective of the system. Both kanban and drum-buffer-rope (DBR) represent synchronized production control approaches. Syn.: synchronous manufacturing. See: synchronous scheduling.
Syn.: synchronized production.

The coordination of activities and resources that require simultaneous operation to meet performance objectives such as meeting demand or maximizing throughput subject to system constraints. Examples include kanban and drum-buffer-rope (DBR) scheduling methods. See: synchronized production.
Syn.: predetermined motion time.
A regularly interacting or interdependent group of items, processes, applications, or entities forming a unified whole that acts toward the achievement of a common goal.

1) In supply chain management (SCM), the resource located at any one of the trading partners that most limits the end-to-end throughput of the supply chain. 2) In information systems, the limitation of an application to perform certain specific functionality.
A facility layout methodology that develops the layout of a facility by considering the importance of proximity of each department to the other departments.
Syn.: nervousness.

1) A method of problem-solving that encompasses the identification, study, and evaluation of interdependent parts and their attributes that function in an ongoing process and that constitute an organic whole. 2) The detailed examination of the information needed for an organization, the characteristics and components of the current information system, and the requirements of any proposed changes to the information system.
The audit of any activity that can affect final product quality.
A perspective in decision-making that emphasizes the overall performance of an entire system instead of the performance of its individual parts. Syn.: systems view.
The integration of multiple computer systems to enable faster data retrieval and increased information system responsiveness.

A philosophy of problem-solving that recognizes the interconnections between the parts of complex systems, views them as a whole, and manages those interactions to improve the performance of the system as a whole.
Syn.: systems concept.
Syn.: takt time.

The purchasing process focused on transactions and nonstrategic material buying. It is closely aligned with the ordering portion of executing the purchasing transaction process. Its characteristics include stable demand with limited fluctuations; defined standard specifications noncritical to production; no delivery issues; and high quality reliability. See: strategic sourcing.
The specific choice made about how to allocate resources and other specific steps and actions necessary to implement a tactical plan. See: tactical plan.

A functional plan (e.g., production plan, sales plan, marketing plan) that breaks down an organization's long-term strategic plan into short-term actions that synchronize activities and resources across functions to achieve intermediate goals and objectives to support the strategic plan. See: aggregate planning, production planning, sales and operations planning (S&OP), strategic plan, tactical planning.

The process of developing a set of tactical plans (e.g., production plan, sales plan, and marketing plan) for synchronized short-term activities designed to meet the organization's overall strategic goals and objectives. See: operational plan, operational planning, production planning, sales and operations planning (S&OP), strategic planning, tactical plan.
Syn.: Taguchi method.

A quality control method conducted at the product and process design stages in the product development cycle that encompasses three phases of product design: system design, parameter design, and tolerance design. The goal is to reduce quality loss by establishing parameters in the product and process development cycle to reduce the overall variability of the product’s physical and performance characteristics. Syn.: Taguchi methodology. See: robust design.

A common clause in procurement contracts that requires the buyer to pay a portion of the agreed-upon contract amount in the form of a penalty if the buyer does not purchase the entire quantity of goods specified in the contract.

The pace of production that is required to match the rate of customer demand, computed as the available production time divided by the rate of customer demand. This rate becomes the heartbeat of any lean production system, representing the rate at which units should complete the production process to meet demand. Syn.: tact time.

An unnecessary action taken to compensate for variation within the control limits of a stable process. When a process is in statistical control, tampering increases rather than decreases variation, as evidenced in the funnel experiment.

1) An outcome that can be quantitatively measured or valued, such as the costs of physical assets. 2) A dimension of service quality referring to the physical appearance of the service facility, including the personnel and equipment.
A freight car with no top, a flat bottom, and fixed sides that is primarily used for hauling bulk commodities.

Raw materials, intermediate materials, or finished goods that are stored in tanks. The description of inventory as tank inventory indicates the necessity of calculating the quantity on hand from the levels within the tanks.
A ship designed to transport liquefied freight.
A rate structure in which a shipping rate increases as the distance shipped increases, but the increases are not directly correlated to the increase in the distance shipped.
If a job is late, the difference between the delivery date and the due date. See: earliness, lateness.
The weight of an empty container, obtained by deducting the net weight of the contents of the container from the gross weight of the full container.

The process of designing a product to meet a specific cost objective. Target costing involves setting the planned selling price and subtracting the desired profit as well as marketing and distribution costs, thus leaving the required manufacturing or target cost.

In a min-max system, the equivalent of the maximum. The target inventory is equal to the order point plus a variable order quantity. This is often called an order-up- to inventory level and is used in a periodic review system. Syn.: order-up-to level.
A definable group of relatively homogeneous customers to whom a company has decided to market its products or services.

The process of focusing marketing activities specifically on those people who are most likely to buy a company’s products and services. Data gathered about people who use the internet enables companies to identify and focus on more likely candidates.
An official schedule of taxes and fees imposed by a country on imports or exports. The additional costs may or may not be passed on to the consumer.

1) In project management, the lowest level to which work can be subdivided on a project. 2) In activity-based cost accounting, a subdivision of an activity representing the smallest amount of work. Tasks are used to describe activities.
Performing multiple tasks concurrently, e.g., assigning multiple picking orders to a single picker to pick concurrently or performing a cycle count of a location while picking an item.

1) In project management, the process of identifying, managing, and controlling the work that must be completed each day to keep the project on schedule. 2) The practice of determining the resources and sequence of tasks necessary to carry out delivery processes, including aggregation and staging of products for shipment.
Abbreviation for time-based competition.
Acronym for triple bottom line.
Acronym for total cost.
Acronym for total cost analysis.
Acronym for total cost of ownership.
Acronym for transmission control protocol/internet protocol.

All work activities required between the end of one operation or job and the start of setup for the next operation or job, with both jobs requiring the same machinery or facilities. See: teardown time.
Syn.: disassembly bill of material (BOM).

The time needed to remove a setup from a machine or facility to restore it to a normal state before the next setup begins. Teardown is an element of manufacturing lead time, but it is often included in setup or run time rather than managed separately. See: teardown.
The transmission of technology (e.g., knowledge, skills, software, and hardware) from one country, organization, business, or entity to another country, organization, business, or entity.
Acronym for total employee involvement.
Transmission of voice and image data at a distance by electronic means.
Syn.: operation overlapping.

In transportation, a location where carriers load and unload goods to consolidate shipments in a transportation network. They also are used to make connections between local pickup and delivery services and line-haul services. Terminals may be owned and operated by the carrier or the public.
A discount provided if freight is delivered to or picked up from the carrier’s terminal.

In ocean transportation, a charge levied on a container by a port for loading or unloading. THCs at the origin or destination port are paid by the shipment's buyer or seller depending on the terms of sale. THCs at transshipment ports are paid by the ocean carrier.
The value of an operation or entity at the end of the period considered.
All the provisions and agreements of a contract.

In international trade, the element of a contract that states the delivery and payment terms between a buyer and a seller. It includes when and where the transfer of goods will occur, documentation that is required, and liabilities for both parties while the goods are in transit.

The portion of a contract of sale that specifies the responsibilities of the seller or exporter and the responsibilities of the buyer or importer, especially the point at which one party’s responsibilities end and the other party’s responsibilities begin (including the point at which risk of loss or damage transfers from the seller to the buyer). These terms are commonly specified using Incoterms.
Acronym for twenty-foot equivalent unit.
Acronym for total factor productivity.
Acronym for terminal handling charge.
The maximum output capability, allowing no adjustments for preventive maintenance, unplanned downtime, shutdown, and so forth.
The amount of time, eliminating all stops, waiting, and additional time due to error, that is needed for one item to go through an entire process.

A holistic management philosophy developed by Dr. Eliyahu M. Goldratt based on the principle that complex systems exhibit inherent simplicity by having, at any given time, only a small number of variables—perhaps only one, known as a constraint—that actually limit the ability to generate more of the system’s goal. Syn.: constraint theory.

A cost and managerial accounting system that accumulates costs and revenues into three areas—throughput, inventory, and operating expense. It does not create incentives (through allocation of overhead) to build up inventory. This accounting method is considered to provide a truer reflection of actual cash flows generated by revenues and costs than traditional cost accounting. TOC accounting provides a simplified and more accurate form of direct costing that subtracts costs that vary with throughput quantity. Unlike traditional cost accounting systems in which the focus is generally placed on reducing costs overall, the primary focus of TOC accounting is on aggressively exploiting the constraint(s) to increase net income. Syns.: constraint accounting, throughput accounting.

A quality-related concept created by W. Edwards Deming. The four aspects of profound knowledge are appreciation of a system, knowledge about variation, theory of knowledge, and knowledge of psychology.

The set of 18 basic movements identified by Frank and Lillian Gilbreth that are used in the study of motion and manual work to identify opportunities to eliminate wasted movement and improve productivity. The name of the term is essentially Gilbreth spelled backwards. Examples of movements include grasp, move, release, select, and position. See: methods study, motion study, predetermined time standards.
Syn.: triple smoothing.

An outsourcing relationship in which an external firm manages or performs part or all of a company's logistics functions, such as transportation, warehousing, distribution, and reverse logistics. See: fourth-party logistics (4PL), reverse logistics service.
A company that manages all or part of another company’s product transportation and distribution operations.
Companies that handle freight transportation and transportation management services for shippers. See: third-party logistics (3PL).
The outsourcing of the warehousing function by the seller of the goods.
Formerly known as the Thomas Register of American Manufacturers, a privately produced reference database that includes a listing of part suppliers by product type and geographic area.

A multidisciplinary approach to develop models of various potential futures, with the goal of anticipating when, where, and how potential threats might occur. The intent is to develop methods for detecting the evolution of threats, thus reducing their risk of occurrence, diminishing their impact, or speeding up recovery from them.

A simple kanban structure for parts purchased from external suppliers that focuses on cycling three bins of material continually and provides a visible method to align replenishment with consumption. One bin is on the factory floor, one is in factory storage, and the third bin is ready to ship from the supplier at all times to protect against stockouts of the purchased items.

A project management technique that uses three cost or duration estimates to stand for the optimistic (O), most likely (M), and pessimistic (P) situations. The mean value (MV) is often found using MV = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6. This technique can improve the accuracy of cost or duration estimates when underlying assumptions are uncertain.

1) The rate at which the system generates goal units, expressed for a given time period, such as per month, week, day, or even minute. If the goal units are money, throughput is an amount of money per time period. In that case, throughput is calculated as revenues received minus total variable costs and then divided by the length of the time period. See: throughput time. 2) In warehousing, the number of goods that are moving through the warehouse at any given moment.

A management accounting method based on the concept that because every system has a constraint that limits global performance, the most effective way to evaluate the impact that any proposed action will have on the system as a whole is to consider the expected changes in the global measures of throughput, inventory, and operating expense. Syn.: theory of constraints (TOC) accounting.
The total time required to complete a process. See: cycle time, manufacturing lead time, throughput.
Acronym for times interest earned.
The group of suppliers and customers with which an organization interacts directly. See: first-tier customer, first-tier supplier.

A strategy used to vary workforce levels in which additional full-time or part-time employees are hired during peak demand periods while a smaller permanent staff is maintained year-round. This technique is used heavily in perishable seasonal goods industries (e.g., chocolate production or nursery plants).
A cross-functional team established to achieve a specific goal within a short time period.
A type of contract that is a hybrid between cost-reimbursable and fixed-time contracts.

A number of days of data summarized into a columnar or row-wise display. For example, a weekly time bucket contains all the relevant data for an entire week. Weekly time buckets are considered to be the largest possible (at least in the near and medium term) to permit effective material requirements planning (MRP). Syn.: bucket.
In manufacturing, a purposeful amount of time incorporated into a production process or schedule to protect against uncertainty such as delays, disruptions, or variability.
A paper or electronic document recording attendance time, often used for indicating the number of hours for which wages are to be paid. Syn.: clock card.

A policy or guideline established to delineate the point where various restrictions or changes in operating procedures take place. For example, changes to the master production schedule (MPS) can be accomplished easily beyond the cumulative lead time, while changes inside the cumulative lead time become increasingly more difficult to a point where changes should be resisted. Time fences can be used to define these points. See: demand time fence (DTF), frozen zone, hedge, planning time fence.

A strategy of holding safety stock based on the usage of the item over a designated time frame, such as a number of days, weeks, or months. Safety stock varies directly with demand rates. This differs from statistical-based safety stocks because the amount is not based on the standard deviation of demand during the lead time.
The technique of planning future demand, supply, and inventories by time period. Material requirements planning (MRP) uses a time phasing approach.

A set of data that is distributed over time, such as demand data in monthly time periods. Various patterns of demand—seasonal, trend, cyclical, and random—must be considered when analyzing time series data.

Analysis of any variable classified by time in which the values of the variable are functions of the time periods. Time series analysis is used in forecasting. A time series consists of seasonal, cyclical, trend, and random components. See: cyclical component, random component, seasonal component, trend component.

A method of forecasting that separates time series data into as many as three predictable components: trend, seasonal, and cyclical. The forecast is created by projecting the predictable patterns individually and then combining them into one forecast. See: cyclical component, random component, seasonal component, trend component.
A forecasting method that projects historical data patterns into the future. It involves the assumption that the near-term future will be like the recent past.
The recording of date and time when a transaction occurs. This is often used for period closings, as well as overall data management.

The predetermined time allowed for the performance of a specific job, task, or process. It often consists of two parts: one for machine setup and one for actual running. A time standard can be developed through observation of the actual work (time study), summation of standard micromotion times (predetermined or synthetic time standards), or approximation (historical job times).
The measurement of how long it takes a worker to complete a task. This is used for setting time standards for use in scheduling, as well as process optimization.
The recording of labor against a particular job. Syn.: job ticket.
The total time required to design, build, and deliver a product or service, from concept to delivery. See: procurement lead time.
The value provided by delivering a product or service to the customer at exactly the right time.

The difference in the valuation of an amount of funds at the present time and the value of that same amount of funds at a future time based on the earning power of investing the same funds at the present time at the prevailing interest rate or required rate of return. See: discount rate, discounted cash flow, net present value (NPV), present value (PV).

A corporate strategy that emphasizes time as the method for achieving and maintaining a sustainable competitive edge. Its characteristics are: (1) Only those lead times that are important to the customers are considered, (2) lead-time reductions must involve decreases in both the mean and the variance, and (3) the lead-time reductions must be achieved through system or process analysis. Reductions in lead times are achieved by changing the processes and the decision structures used to design, produce, and deliver products to the customers. TBC involves design, manufacturing, and logistical processes.
Syn.: fixed order interval inventory model.
A premium transportation service option that guarantees delivery of goods and services by specific day and time.

A material requirements planning (MRP)–like time planning logic technique for independent demand items in which gross requirements come from a forecast, not via explosion. This method can be used to plan distribution center (DC) inventories as well as to plan for service (repair) parts because MRP logic can readily handle items with dependent demand, independent demand, or a combination of both. It is an approach that uses time periods, thus allowing for lumpy withdrawals instead of average demand. When used in distribution environments, the planned order releases are input into the master schedule dependent demand requirements. See: fixed order quantity (FOQ) inventory model.
The measurement of how well an organization can cover the interest charges on its debts. It is calculated as earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) divided by interest expense.
A published schedule showing times for departures and arrivals between locations.
Acronym for truckload.
Acronym for transportation management system.
Acronym for theory of constraints.
Acronym for trailer on a flatcar.
An allowable difference from an established nominal value that is deemed acceptable for the functioning of the good or service over its life cycle.

1) The upper and lower extreme value permitted by a tolerance. Syn.: specification limit. See: lower specification limit (LSL), upper specification limit (USL). 2) In work measurement, the limit between which a specified operation time value or other work unit will be expected to vary.

The effect of accumulating two or more individual component tolerances within an assembly. Even though each component tolerance may be within the limits, the cumulative tolerance may cause the entire assembly to fail.

A measurement of freight transportation which multiplies the overall weight being transported (in tons) by the distance it is being transported (in miles). It is heavily used in rail and water transportation modes to analyze the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of the mode.
Syn.: calibration frequency.
Syn.: tool order.
The identification number assigned to reference and control a specific tool.
A document authorizing issue of specific tools from the tool crib or other storage. Syn.: tool issue order.

In the total quality management (TQM) philosophy, participation of the highest levels in the organization’s quality improvement efforts. Participation includes establishing and serving on a quality committee, establishing quality policies and goals, deploying those goals to lower levels of the organization, providing the resources and training that the lower levels need to achieve the goals, participating in quality improvement teams, reviewing organization-wide progress, recognizing those who have performed well, and revising the current reward system to reflect the importance of achieving the quality goals.
The total value of all direct materials received in a calendar year. In a lean environment, this number should be very close to the direct material cost that was incurred in the same calendar year.

The concept of taking into consideration all expenditures required to provide a product or service. It includes the sum of total fixed costs as well as total variable costs and enables the definition of average cost.

The process of identifying all costs associated with a product or service in its product life cycle. This includes the costs of acquisition, transportation, storage and handling, order processing, and quality control.

1) In cost-volume-profit (breakeven) analysis, the total cost curve is composed of total fixed and variable costs per unit multiplied by the number of units provided. Breakeven quantity occurs where the total cost curve and total sales revenue curve intersect. See: break-even chart, break- even point. 2) In inventory management, the total cost curve for an item is the sum of the costs of acquiring and carrying the item. See: economic order quantity (EOQ).

The sum of all the costs associated with every activity of the supply stream for a product or service. It provides an insight into the portion that each function contributes, e.g., the costs of acquisition, carrying, transportation, etc.
A sum that includes costs associated with rework, scrap, warranty costs, and other costs associated with preventing or resolving quality problems.

A curve that suggests there is some optimal quality level, denoted as Q*. The curve is calculated by adding costs of internal and external failures, prevention costs, and appraisal costs. The optimal quality level occurs when this curve reaches a minimum point. It is a single turning point curve that always has a minimum.

The sum of the supply chain cost to produce and deliver products and services to customers. It includes the direct and indirect costs to plan the supply chain; source materials, products, goods, merchandise, and services; produce, manufacture, remanufacture, refurbish, repair, and maintain goods and services; manage orders, customer inquiries, and returns; and deliver products and services at the agreed location (point of revenue). See: total supply chain management cost.
The total time required to complete a manufacturing process for a product, from initial processing through final packaging.
An empowerment program in which employees are encouraged to actively participate in planning, problem-solving, and decision-making activities that were traditionally reserved for management.

A measure of productivity of a department, plant, strategic business unit, or firm that measures the efficiency of transforming all inputs, (including labor, capital, energy, material, and equipment,) into outputs of products or services. These individual factor productivities are often combined by weighting each according to its monetary value and then adding them.
Costs that remain constant in total, regardless of changes in activity.
In project management, the length of time an activity can be late without delaying succeeding activities. See: float, free float, independent float.

The ability to continuously schedule and allocate scarce resources to optimally execute production and operational activities based on operations command center insights to increase visibility and coordination of machines, people and processes across the network ecosystem.
A structured approach to maintenance that focuses on regular inspections and tasks to prevent breakdowns, equipment inefficiencies, and to minimize downtime. See: total productive maintenance (TPM).

A maintenance philosophy that incorporates continuing efforts to adapt, modify, and refine equipment to increase flexibility; reduce materials handling; and promote continuous flows. It is operator-oriented maintenance with the involvement of all qualified employees in all maintenance activities. See: total preventive maintenance (TPM).

A system of integrating the quality development, quality maintenance, and quality improvement efforts in an organization to enable production and service at the most economical levels that allow full customer satisfaction.

The discipline of designing quality into the product and manufacturing processes by understanding the needs of the customer and performance capabilities of the equipment. See: design for quality (DFQ), total quality management (TQM).

A management approach to quality improvement that is driven through customer satisfaction. TQM is based on the participation of all members of an organization in improving processes, goods, services, and the culture in which they work. The methods for implementing this approach are found in teachings of such quality leaders as Philip B. Crosby, W. Edwards Deming, Kaoru Ishikawa, J.M. Juran, and Genichi Taguchi. See: manufacturing philosophy, product quality, total quality engineering (TQE).

The total cost to manage order processing, acquire materials, manage inventory, and manage supply chain finance, planning and information technology (IT) costs, as represented as a percentage of revenue. It is calculated as: (Order Management Costs + Material Acquisition Costs + Inventory Carrying Costs + Supply Chain–related Finance and Planning Costs + Total Supply Chain–related IT Costs) ÷ Total Product Revenue. See: total cost to serve.
Evaluating the value of a product or service by assessing its use against the cost. It is used to identify and eliminate unnecessary costs that do not increase the value perceived by the customer.
Costs that vary in total in proportion to changes in activity.
The comprehensive handling of all wastes generated by an organization, from collection to disposal, including following all aspects of compliance and sustainability.

A statistic that is used to determine efficiency for costing or pricing functions. A touch occurs anytime a labor activity is utilized during the manufacturing or service-creation process. This concept has generated the term touch labor for direct labor personnel.
Syn.: direct labor.
A manufacturing methodology developed at Toyota Motor Corporation that has evolved into the concepts of just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing and lean production.
1) Acronym for total productive maintenance. 2) Acronym for total preventive maintenance.
Acronym for time-phased order point.
Acronym for Toyota Production System.
Acronym for total quality control.
Acronym for total quality engineering.
Acronym for total quality management.

1) The ability to track the ongoing location of a shipment. See: supply chain visibility. 2) The registering and tracking of parts, processes, and materials used in production, by lot or serial number. 3) The ability to track the origin of a product back to its raw material(s).
A request to a transportation line to trace a shipment to expedite its movement or to verify delivery.
Directly associating specific costs to a cost object, such as an activity or material. The objective is to understand how costs are generated from business activities.
The process of determining and reporting the location of a shipment throughout the supply chain channel.

Adding capacity in small amounts to attempt to respond to changing demand in real time in the marketplace. This approach may satisfy total demand and help minimize unit costs, but it can be difficult in some situations to add incremental amounts of capacity, especially if the facility has no more space available. See: capacity planning, production planning.

A measure used to evaluate whether the actual demand reflects the forecasting method’s assumptions about demand behavior. It is the ratio of the cumulative forecast errors to the mean absolute deviation (MAD). See: forecast error.

An agreement between or among countries intended to reduce or remove barriers to trade within member countries. Frequently, but not always, those countries are geographically close. Examples of trade blocs are the European Union and the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Syn.: trading bloc.
A deduction from the established price for goods or services that a manufacturer offers to resellers such as wholesalers or retailers. See: price break.
Knowledge about a manufacturing process that gives the owner an advantage over competitors who do not have it. Trade secrets are legally protectable.
Syn.: trade bloc.
An intermediary company that facilitates trade between foreign buyers and sellers and arranges all product export and import details, documentation, and transportation.
An entity external to an organization that is part of its global supply chain. The relationship facilitates the buying and selling of goods and services across borders.
A contract between trading partners that describes all facets of their business together. It is a legal and binding agreement suitable for legal purposes as well as standard working agreements.
A department or function charged with the responsibility for arranging the most economic classification and method of shipment for both incoming and outgoing materials and products.
The area of an organization that plans and executes shipping requirements.
The control of transportation carriers, modes, and services.
A specialized form of containerization in which motor and rail transport coordinate. Syn.: piggyback. See: multimodal solution.
An item used to facilitate training, including charts, graphs, slides, videos, and schematics.
A distribution network that deals with change of ownership of goods and services including the activities of negotiation, selling, and contracting.
An individual event or activity reported to the system, such as issues, receipts, transfers, adjustments, or sales.
The quantity of an item moved between sequential work centers during production. See: batch, overlap quantity.

The price that one part of an organization (subunit, department, division, etc.) charges another part of the same organization for goods or services. Transfer prices are also used in conjunction with one division shipping goods to a customer on behalf of another division. Syn.: transfer pricing. See: interplant transfer.
Syn.: transfer price.

The process that describes the activities associated with the scheduling and creation of products in various types of environments (like make-to-stock (MTS), make-to-order (MTO), and engineer-to-order (ETO) environments). In the Supply Chain Operations Reference Digital Standard (SCOR DS), transform is applied to production; assembly; disassembly; maintenance, repair, and operating (MRO); and services.
The process of converting inputs into finished goods or services. In a service firm, the input may be a customer. See: manufacturing process, production process.
Style of leadership that focuses on empowering people to identify and drive change through vision, inspiration and calls to action.
Syn.: phantom bill of material (BOM).
A temporary condition when the variables in a system or process have changed but not reached steady state yet. Data is usually not collected from the model until less erratic behavior emerges.
Syn.: in-transit inventory.
A service provided by a shipper that allows the purchasing company to stop a shipment mid-route to allow changes to the delivery but to pay the nonstop rate.
A standard allowance that is assumed on any given order for the movement of items from one operation to the next. Syn.: travel time.
Software that converts business data into an electronic data interchange standard format and vice versa.

A confirmation from the receiver of a transmission notifying the sender that the transmission was received error-free. transmission control protocol/internet protocol (TCP/IP)– The communication protocol used by the internet and other computer networks.
The practice of a company allowing external entities, typically customers, to see some internal information, such as order status or inventory levels.
Syn.: pipeline stock.
The function of planning, scheduling, controlling, and executing activities related to mode, vendor, and movement of inventories into, within, and out of an organization.
Syn.: freight broker.
A logistics performance measure of the lead time required for a product to reach its final destination. It is the time between leaving a warehouse and arriving at the destination.
Inventory that is in transit between locations. See: pipeline stock, transit inventory.
A legal regulatory classification of transportation by product, shipping size, rates, carriers, and types of services.
The process of executing requirements for the planning, scheduling, and budgeting of transportation assets, services, and related systems of the shipping process through delivery.

A computer application system designed to plan, execute, and manage transportation operations. This type of application typically includes modules focused on specific functions, such as intermodal transportation, import and export management, fleet service management, and load planning and optimization. See: route management system.
Syn.: mode of transportation.
Evaluating the efficiency of inbound or outbound transportation modes to better match supply and demand, optimize inventory balances, and minimize costs.
Syn.: transit time.
Syn.: shop traveler.
Common stock that has been repurchased by the issuing company.

1) A management technique used to analyze a situation in increasing detail. It illustrates the range of tasks to be accomplished to achieve a primary goal and supporting subgoals. 2) In theory of constraints (TOC), a diagram relating effects to underlying causes. See: current reality tree (CRT), future reality tree (FRT).
General upward or downward movement of a variable over time (e.g., demand or process attribute).
A component of demand, usually describing the impact of increasing or decreasing growth on demand. See: time series analysis, time series decomposition.
A control chart in which the deviation of the subgroup average (X-bar) from an expected trend in the process level is used to evaluate the stability of a process.
A method for forecasting sales data when a definite upward or downward pattern exists. Models include double exponential smoothing, regression, and triple smoothing.
A form of exponential smoothing forecasting that includes a factor for increasing or decreasing trends in the data resulting from variables such as population growth or income changes.
A freight trip of more than two legs used to coordinate movement of materials and goods between manufacturers, suppliers, and customers.
Syn.: order point.

An approach that measures the economic, social, and environmental impact of an organization’s activities with the intent of creating value for both its shareholders and society. The three dimensions are often referred to as people, planet, profit.
A method of exponential smoothing used to forecast products that have both seasonality and accelerating or decelerating trends. Syn.: third-order smoothing.
A carrier that only delivers in full- truckload shipments. If less than a truckload is consumed, the carrier would still charge for a full truckload.
A truck shipment that qualifies for a lower freight rate because it meets a minimum weight and/or volume.

An agile estimating technique for determining the effort needed to complete a task. Instead of estimating exact hours, familiar clothing sizes (e.g., XS, S, M, L, XL, and XXL) are used to reflect a range of scope, complexity, and capacity required for the task.
Acronym for time to market.
Syn.: setup cost.
Syns.: cycle time, setup.
A system, operation, project, contract, or software application that is already prepared and ready for immediate use.
1) Syn.: inventory turnover. 2) In financial terms, the annual sales volume. 3) In the workplace, the rate at which employees leave and are replaced.
An indicator of whether or not a company is using its assets efficiently. It is measured by dividing sales by average assets during a particular period.
Syn.: inventory turnover.

A measurement used to describe the carrying capacity of a cargo ship or a terminal’s handling capacity. One TEU equals a standard 20-foot x 8-foot x 8-foot (length x width x height) shipping container.
Acronym for total waste management.

A type of fixed order quantity (FOQ) technique in which inventory is carried in two bins. A replenishment quantity is ordered when the first bin is empty. During the replenishment lead time, material is used from the second bin, which contains a quantity to cover demand. This term also is used to loosely describe any fixed-order system even when physical bins do not exist. Syn.: bin reserve system. See: visual review system.

A kanban system in which both a move card and production card are used. The move card is attached to the standard container and authorizes the movement of a specific number of parts from a source to a point of use. The production card authorizes the production of a given number of parts for use or replenishment. Syn.: dual-card kanban system. See: one-card kanban system.

A master-scheduling approach in which a planning bill of material (BOM) is used to master schedule an end product or family, along with selected key features (options and accessories). See: hedge, multilevel master schedule, production forecast.
An incorrect decision to reject something (such as a statistical hypothesis or a lot of products) when it is acceptable. See: producer’s risk (Σ).
An incorrect decision to accept something when it is unacceptable. See: consumer risk (ß).
A control chart for evaluating the stability of a process in terms of the average count of events of a given classification per unit occurring in a sample. Syn.: count-per-unit chart.

word: U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB)
definition: An independent, non-regulatory federal agency that investigates significant chemical accidents in an effort to determine their underlying cause.

A law enforcement agency within the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Its primary mission is to prevent people from entering the country illegally or bringing anything harmful or illegal into the United States.
An executive department of the U.S. federal government charged with overseeing federal transportation projects and setting safety regulations for all major forms of transportation.

An independent executive agency of the U.S. federal government tasked with developing and enforcing environmental regulations, protecting people from significant health risks, and sponsoring research about the environment.

An agency of the U.S. department of Health and Human Services charged with assuring foods are safe and properly labelled. The FDA also ensures that veterinary drugs and that human vaccines, biological products, and medical devices are safe and effective.
Acronym for upper control limit.
Acronym for undesirable effect. Pronounced “oodee.”
Acronym for uniform delivered pricing.
Acronym for unified extensible firmware interface.
Acronym for unit of issue.

A production line set up to resemble the letter U. The shape allows workers to easily perform several nonsequential tasks with minimal non-value-added movement and promotes communication among workers. The number of workstations in a U-line is usually determined by line balancing. See: cellular layout.
Acronym for United Nations.

A framework for guiding companies through the process of formally committing to, assessing, defining, implementing, measuring, and communicating the United Nations Global Compact and its principles. See: United Nations (UN) Global Compact.
The portion of the production capability that cannot be attained. This is typically caused by factors such as equipment unavailability, suboptimal scheduling, or resource limitations.

A shipment that is not evenly spread out on or within a piece of transportation equipment that can lead to instability and handling problems in transit because of the overloading of specific axles or wheels.
