Unknown future events that cannot be predicted quantitatively within useful limits, such as an accident that destroys facilities, a major strike, or an innovation that makes existing products obsolete.
In the environment of a production system, a factor that cannot be changed (e.g., temperature, natural causes, weather, or vibration).

Allowing more time than should be necessary to complete a day’s work. As a result, a daily quota is met more often and workers have time to cross-train or perform maintenance on their tools and machines.
A condition occurring when more personnel or hours are allocated to a job than are required to produce the planned output.
In theory of constraints (TOC), any negative aspect of an environment that is noted so that a current reality tree may be constructed.
An activity by management or labor that violates the U.S. National Labor Relations Act. Failure to bargain in good faith is an example.
The defined architecture of the platform firmware that is used to boot computer hardware.

A comprehensive set of laws governing all commercial transactions in the United States. While not a federal law, it is uniformly adopted by most states, which allows businesses to enter into contracts with the confidence that the terms will be enforced the same way in every jurisdiction.
A pricing policy in which all customers pay the same delivered price regardless of their locations. A company allocates the total transportation cost among all customers.
In a lean production environment, the distribution of work among work centers so that the time required for each operation to complete all tasks is as close to equal as possible. See: line balancing.
A retail product numbering and barcoding system that identifies the item and the manufacturer.
A type of web address that identifies a resource, its location, and the means of retrieving it. See: web page.
A U.S. act that provides a framework for regulating public warehousing. It sets up the legal responsibilities of warehouse managers and determines the receipts that can be issued.
A formal contract between a company and the union representing its employees, usually covering two to six years, that covers all aspects of pay, working conditions, and strike options.
A designation that indicates that a company or operation does not have a union contract.

A facility in which all hourly employees are unionized. More formally, it is a clause in a collective bargaining agreement under which membership in the union is required as a condition of employment. Union shops are illegal in some regions.

The cost of one unit of an item or service. For a manufactured part, the cost would be the total labor, material, and overhead cost for one unit of production (e.g., one part, one gallon or one pound). See: cost of goods sold (COGS).

A shipping unit made up of multiple items, such as a pallet or container. Material is arranged so the items can be picked up or moved as a single unit, reducing materials handling, storage, or transportation costs. A unit load is often shrink-wrapped on a pallet before shipment.
A standard measure of time, such as a minute or hour, used in logistics to identify transportation quantities.
The standard quantity of an item requested or supplied to a user, such as from inventory storage locations.
The unit in which the quantity of an item is managed, such as sold, purchased, or stored in inventory. Examples include pounds, each, box of 12, package of 20, gallons, etc.
A standard conversion ratio that converts one unit of measure to another (e.g., one case equals 20 eaches). It is often used to increase efficiency when entering customer or purchase orders.

A method of depreciation whereby the amount to be recovered (written off as a period expense) is calculated based on the estimated life of the equipment in units to be produced over the life and the number of units produced in a given time period. United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International

A multilateral treaty that governs the sale of goods internationally. It facilitates international trade and removes legal barriers by providing uniform rules for commercial transactions. It is sometimes known as the Vienna Convention.

A voluntary initiative whereby companies embrace, support, and enact, within their sphere of influence, a set of core values in the areas of human rights, labor standards, the environment, and anticorruption. United Nations Standard Products and Services Code®
A global, open standard for classifying products and services across sectors using a hierarchy based on segment, family, class, and commodity information.
A trade agreement between the three countries of North America formed in 2020, replacing the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).
The consolidation of boxes, cartons, and packages into one larger unit to make handling, identification, and transportation easier and more efficient. See: containerization, palletization.
A sales metric, often used in the retail sector, to measure the average number of items that customers are purchasing in a given transaction.

A standardized barcode symbology consisting of a unique 12-digit number that is used to identify products in retail sales channels. The barcode can be scanned at the point of sale (POS) to facilitate transaction processing and inventory management. See: model number.
The strategy of designing a product initially intended for one market in such a way that it can also be sold in other markets. This is a form of standardization.
The population, or large set of data, from which samples are drawn. It is usually assumed to be infinitely large or at least very large relative to the sample.
A transaction that updates the quantity on hand but for which no allocation exists, such as replacements for damaged goods or unexpected demand.
An order generated outside of the forecast, usually based on unforeseen demand or trends.
A receipt transaction that updates the quantity on hand but for which no order exists, such as free or promotional samples.
Repair tasks that occur due to unanticipated equipment failure or as a result of remanufacturing teardown.
Acronym for United Nations Standard Products and Services Code®.
1) Acronym for universal product code. 2) Acronym for uniform product code.
An additional charge added to a price that was not included in the original contract. Examples include additional freight or fuel costs or special customer requests. Syn.: surcharge.
An improvement to a product's or resource's functionality or characteristics by adding or replacing components.
Control limit for points above the central line in a control chart.
In statistical process control (SPC), the line that defines the maximum acceptable level of random output. See: tolerance limit.

A sales strategy that encourages customers to purchase more expensive items or upgraded versions of the product they were planning to buy. Upselling can generate higher amounts of revenue from an existing customer base.

The ability of a facility to quickly increase its output and capacity to deliver for the foreseeable future in order to meet a non-forecasted increase in demand. The main drivers of this flexibility are the availability of direct labor and/or direct materials and the actual production capacity of the facility.
A discrete measurement of the quantity of increased production a supply chain can achieve and sustain for 30 days in response to unplanned demand.
A discrete measurement of how quickly a supply chain can respond to an unplanned increase in demand without an impact to service or cost.
Used as a relative reference within a firm or supply chain to indicate moving in the direction of the raw material supplier. Ant.: downstream.

The recovery of valuable materials from waste streams such as construction and demolition waste, industrial waste, and end-of-life products. Urban mining contributes to the circular economy through the use of these reclaimed materials in production processes.
Acronym for uniform resource locator.
The number of units or dollars of an inventory item consumed over a period of time.
A measurement of the frequency or speed that product is used over a specific period of time.
Deviation of the actual consumption of materials as compared with the standard.
The acceptance of a product or material in its current state, even though it may not conform to specifications.
The portion of a computer application through which the end user interacts. This may include the keyboard, mouse, touch screen, and other peripheral devices.
A characteristic of computer software or hardware that makes it easy for the user or operator to use the programs or equipment with a minimum of specialized knowledge.

A process layout in which the sequence of activities is arranged in the shape of a U. The first and last stages of the process are in close proximity to one another, and workers can easily communicate or move from one work area to another. See: work cell.
Acronym for upper specification limit.
Acronym for United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

1) A measure that compares actual time used to available time. Traditionally, it is calculated as the ratio of direct time charged (run time plus setup time) to the clock time available. Utilization is a percentage between 0 percent and 100 percent that reflects the amount of time lost due to the unavailability of machines, tools, workers, etc. See: available time, efficiency, productivity. 2) In theory of constraints, activation of a resource that productively contributes to reaching the goal. Over-activation of a resource does not productively utilize a resource.
Acronym for the Uniform Warehouse Receipts Act.

The technique of determining worth, typically of inventory. Valuation of inventories may be expressed in standard dollars, replacement dollars, current average dollars, or last- purchase-price dollars.
The worth of an item, good, or service. Value is often determined by what the customer is willing to pay.

A technique of determining the value of each required function of a product or service, in order to ensure and enhance customer satisfaction. The objective is to concentrate on those functions desired by the customer and reduce costs by eliminating non-value-added functions. Syn.: value engineering. See: value perspective.

The sum of the probability of risk events multiplied by the monetary impact of events. A risk event is defined as a deviation from the expected metrics value for the process. See: overall value at risk (VAR).
The tasks required to provide goods or services to a customer, including operations, logistics, marketing, and service.
An examination of all activities a company uses to produce and deliver its products and services. The objective is to identify areas where costs can be reduced and value and efficiency improved.
A collaborative global forum that provides best practices to assist companies in reducing their greenhouse gas emissions.

An interconnected set of organizations that collaborate to provide products or services to the end consumer, such as suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and retailers. The objective is to improve customer satisfaction while minimizing costs.
Syn.: value analysis.

A measure that uses the performance and importance scores for various dimensions of performance for an item or service to calculate a score that indicates the overall value of the item or service to a customer.
A pricing strategy that determines the price based on the perceived value to the customer of the product or service, rather than the cost of manufacturing or delivering to the customer.
A method of determining how well a product or service meets a need, based on the interpretation of value by an individual or group. See: value analysis.

The processes encompassed in the creation, production, and delivery of a good or service to the market. The value stream begins with the concept or need and includes suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, service producers, and support personnel. A value stream focuses on the customer and may be controlled by a single business or a network of several businesses.
A graph displaying the sequence of operations needed to produce and deliver a product or service.

A lean production tool to visually understand the flow of materials from supplier to customer that includes the current process and flow as well as the value- added and non-value-added time of all the process steps. It is used to help reduce waste, decrease flow time, and make the process flow more efficient and effective.

1) In accounting, the addition of direct labor, direct material, and allocated overhead assigned at an operation. It is the cost roll-up as a component goes through a manufacturing process to finished goods inventory. 2) In manufacturing, the actual increase of utility from the viewpoint of the customer as a component is transformed from raw material to finished goods inventory. It also refers to the contribution made by an operation or a plant to the final usefulness and value of a product, as seen by the customer. The objective is to eliminate all non-value-added activities in producing and providing a good or service. See: non-value-added.
A third-party network providing additional services to companies, such as electronic data interchange (EDI).

A measurement that indicates the economic value contributed to an organization by the employees. It is used to assess workforce productivity and resource allocation and is calculated by adding operating profit to salaries, wages, and payroll expenses and then dividing by the average number of employees.

An intermediary between an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and end customers. The VAR enhances the hardware and software it obtains from OEMs by adding value for the end customer through bundling or customization.

A type of tax that is assessed incrementally and levied on the price of a product or service at each stage of production, distribution, or sale to the end consumer. The tax is carefully tracked in returns, and routes are optimized to minimize tax, duty, and value-added tax considerations. This tax is known in some countries as a goods and services tax. See: foreign/free trade zone (FTZ).

A management approach that focuses on aligning all levels of an organization to maximize shareholder value, Decision-making and management processes are based on a long-term perspective and creation of value. See: economic value added (EVA), net present value (NPV).
An organization that is designed and managed to add value from the viewpoint of the customer in the transformation of raw materials into a finished good or service.
Acronym for value-added network.
1) Acronym for value at risk. 2) Acronym for value-added reseller.
Any quantity or value that can exist in different amounts or types. Ant.: constant.
An operating expenditure that varies based on the number of units produced. See: fixed cost.

An inventory valuation method in which only variable production costs are applied to the product and not fixed costs such as factory overhead. Variable costing can be helpful for internal management analysis but is not widely accepted for external financial reporting. For make-or-buy decisions, variable costing should be used rather than full absorption costing. Syn.: direct costing.
Any type of information that can be measured and recorded numerically. Variable data is often used in quality control and statistical analysis reporting. See: attribute data.

All manufacturing costs, other than direct labor and direct materials, that vary directly with production volume. Variable overhead is necessary to produce the product but cannot be directly assigned to a specific product. See: fixed overhead.
The condition that occurs when the output of a process is not consistently repeatable in quantity, quality, or a combination of both.

A type of acceptance sampling where the numerical magnitude of a characteristic is measured and recorded for each inspected unit. This type of sampling involves reference to a continuous scale of some kind.
1) The difference between the expected (budgeted or planned) value and the actual value. 2) In statistics, a measurement of dispersion of data. See: estimate of error.
A change in data, a characteristic, or a function that is caused by one of four factors: special causes, common causes, tampering, or structural variation.

In theory of constraints, a procedure for determining the general flow of parts and products from raw materials to finished products. A V logical structure starts with one or a few raw materials, and the product expands into a number of different products as it flows through divergent points in its routings. The shape of an A logical structure reflects many raw materials fabricated and assembled into a few finished products. A T logical structure consists of numerous similar finished products assembled from common assemblies, subassemblies, and parts. An I logical structure is the simplest of production flows, in which resources are shared between or among different products and the flow is in a straight-line sequence (e.g., an assembly line).
Acronym for value-based management.
Acronym for Value Chain Initiative.
A machine used to transport goods. Vehicles are used in all forms of transportation, except for pipeline.

1) The rate of change of an item with respect to time. See: inventory turnover, lead time. 2) In supply chain management (SCM), a term used to indicate the relative speed of all transactions, collectively, within a supply chain community. A maximum velocity is most desirable because it indicates higher asset turnover for stockholders and faster order-to-delivery response for customers.
Any seller of a product or service in the marketplace. See: supplier.
Syn.: supplier lead time.
The act of measuring the vendor’s performance. Measurements usually cover delivery reliability, lead time, quality, and price. See: supplier measurement.
Syn.: supplier scheduler.
Syn.: supplier scheduling.

A means of optimizing supply chain performance in which the supplier has access to the customer’s inventory data and is responsible for maintaining the inventory level required by the customer. Based upon an agreed- to service level and inventory performance objectives, the supplier monitors inventory activity and levels and plans for and replenishes its customer's inventory with minimal transactional involvement by the customer. The vendor invoices the customer based on the replenishment that occurs. See: co-managed inventory (CMI), continuous replenishment, scan-based trading (SBT), supplier-managed inventory.
Syn.: consignment inventory.
A group of individuals assigned outside normal channels to develop ideas for new products, services, or business models that extend beyond the organization’s core business operations.
The sharing of information and responsibility for supply chain planning and execution between customers and suppliers. See: vertical integration.

The relationship between a parent item and a component in its bill of material (BOM) that defines the need for the component based on producing the parent, without regard to the availability of other components at the same level in the BOM. See: horizontal dependency.

A method of displaying or printing output from a material requirements planning (MRP) system in which requirements, scheduled receipts, projected balance, and so forth are displayed vertically. Vertical displays are often used in conjunction with bucket-less systems.

The degree to which a firm produces multiple value-adding stages from raw material to the sale of the product to the ultimate consumer. The degree of vertical integration increases as the firm performs more stages of the process. See: backward integration, forward integration.
The strategy of tailoring a narrow set of products or services to a specific niche customer market.

A distribution channel structure where manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers work together to meet end customer needs, reduce conflicts, and improve efficiency through strong contracts or the efforts of a large coordinating channel member.
An online marketplace connecting buyers and sellers within the same industry. It enables lower prices by lowering transaction costs.
The legal combination of two firms at different levels of the supply chain, such as when one firm was a supplier to the other.
A part storage and retrieval system that uses vertical racks to store items and an automated storage/ retrieval system to insert and retrieve those items.
An organization with functions that were previously performed by suppliers but are now accomplished internally. See: horizontally integrated firm.

A variant of job rotation in which a separate work area is set up for a trainee so that the actual work situation does not pressure the trainee. Examples are cockpit simulators and other machine simulators.
A software program that uses language processing and artificial intelligence (AI) to provide automated services or guidance. See: chatbot.

A logical rather than physical grouping of manufacturing resources. Resources in virtual cells can be dispersed throughout a facility. Product mix changes may change the layout of a virtual cell. This technique is used when it is not practical to move the equipment.
Syn.: virtual organization.

1) A digital representation of a physical factory that includes analytical tools that can be used to simulate and optimize production operations and decisions in response to changing conditions. See: digital twin. 2) A temporary network of production facilities owned by different organizations that are coordinated by an integrated system to design, produce, and deliver a product. See: virtual organization.
An application that provides updated information about inventory levels and status across a network of locations and enables remote execution of orders and inventory releases.

A short-term alliance between independent organizations in a potentially long-term relationship to design, produce, and distribute a product. Organizations cooperate based on mutual values and act as a single entity to third parties. Syn.: virtual corporation. See: virtual factory.

The process of using interactive, computer- generated experiences (hardware and software) that take place within a simulated environment for the purposes of training personnel or handling dangerous jobs remotely. VR technology incorporates auditory and visual feedback that helps with completing tasks or experiencing a realistic training simulation.

1) A digital representation of a physical supply chain that provides visibility and can predict future events and disruptions. See: digital twin. 2) A network of firms that typically exists for only a short period of time to respond to a specific supply chain need or event. Once the task or project is complete, the virtual supply chain is dissolved, and another network of new partners is created to address the next issue that arises.
An online trading exchange that enables both information integration and collaboration among multiple trading partners.

1) The application of digital technology to provide visibility to inventory stored in multiple stocking locations and real-time decision-making tools to fulfill demand in a way that minimizes cost and maximizes service. 2) A non- physical warehouse used to designate an inventory location for a specific purpose, e.g., rework inventory that is physically in one warehouse but shows in a non-allocatable virtual warehouse.
The ability to view important information throughout a facility or supply chain no matter where in the facility or supply chain the information is located.

The shared perception of the organization’s future—what the organization will achieve and a supporting philosophy. This shared vision must be supported by strategic objectives, strategies, and action plans to move it in the desired direction. See: vision statement.
The organization’s statement of its shared perception of the future. See: vision.
The process of developing a plan for how an organization will perform in the future.
The use of visual indicators such as colors, signs, and diagrams to quickly communicate current process status to workers, enabling effective decision-making and reducing errors.
A non-destructive inspection method that uses the human eye or other visual tools to examine a product or component for defects, damage, or non-conformance to standards.
A management system in which every metric that matters, standardized work, and improvement approaches are displayed on the shop floor and in the office.

A simple inventory control system in which the inventory replenishments are determined by a physical review of the amount of on-hand inventory. This system is usually used for low-value items, such as nuts and bolts. See: two-bin inventory system.
The application of Pareto's law to the quality management process of identifying significant causes of observed effects. See: 80-20 rule.
Acronym for vendor-managed inventory.
Acronym for voice of the customer.
Acronym for vendor-owned inventory.
The functions and features that external customers desire for goods and services. See: design for six sigma (DFSS), form-fit-function, quality function deployment (QFD).
Syn.: pick-to-voice system.
Syn.: pick-to-voice system.
A type of price break received by ordering goods in larger quantities.
The ability of the transformation process to quickly accommodate large variations in production levels.
The strategy of buying in large quantities to take advantage of volume price or shipping discounts.
An internal document that contains all the supporting documents related to services performed or goods purchased and authorizes payment to the supplier.
Acronym for virtual reality.
Acronym for value stream mapping.
A hybrid project management methodology that leverages the best of both the governance of waterfall and the flexibility of agile methods. See: agile project management, waterfall project management.

A dynamic lot-sizing technique that evaluates all possible ways of ordering to cover net requirements in each period of the planning horizon to arrive at the theoretically optimum ordering strategy to minimize the total cost of the entire net requirements schedule. See: discrete order quantity, dynamic lot sizing.
The time a job remains at a work center after an operation is completed until it is moved to the next operation.
Syn.: queuing theory.
Authorization to accept an item that, during production or upon inspection, is found to depart from specified requirements but nevertheless is considered suitable for use as is or after rework.

A warehouse truck that uses a motor to perform lift and movement of heavy loads. There are many forms of walkie vehicles, each with differing operational and physical configurations depending on its intended work area and task requirements.
Syn.: pilot test.
A complete count of all units currently held in inventory at a specific location to provide accurate stock levels at a specific time. See: four-wall inventory, physical inventory.
Acronym for wide area network.
A device used to scan a barcode in order to identify a product and its details.
An undesirable effect in which the bottleneck moves frequently from one resource to another, which makes it difficult to concentrate process improvement efforts.
A facility where goods and materials are stored in anticipation of demand or disposition.

The utilization of mechanical or electronic devices to complete tasks related to storing, retrieving, and moving inventory as a substitute for labor resources to generate cost savings, to achieve added security, to reduce injuries, and to keep workers out of sensitive environments.

1) The need for storage and distribution space to meet a firm's required logistics throughput. 2) The need for an item to replenish stock at a branch warehouse. See: distribution requirements planning (DRP).

A computer application system designed to manage and optimize workflows and the storage of goods within a warehouse, including receiving and storing goods, fulfilling orders, shipping, and tracking movement. It often interfaces with automated data capture, enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, and robotics.
The activities related to storing and handling goods within a facility before their use or their transport to another location within the supply chain.

1) An expressed or implied promise by a seller or third-party provider to repair or replace a product if it does not meet established conditions over a specified period of time. 2) A commitment, either expressed or implied, that a certain fact regarding the subject matter of a contract is presently true or will be true. A warranty is different from a guarantee, which refers to a contract or promise by an entity to answer for the performance of a product or person. See: guarantee, special warranty.
A cost associated with servicing a warranty, including shipping, receiving, repairing, replacement, and the materials needed for repair or replacement.
An implied warranty that goods are fit for the use to which they are generally applied.

1) Any activity that does not add value to the good or service in the eyes of the consumer. See: seven wastes. 2) A by-product of a process or task with unique characteristics requiring special management control. Waste production can usually be planned and somewhat controlled. Scrap is typically not planned and may result from the same production run as waste. See: hazardous waste.

1) Arrangement in which companies exchange their wastes for the benefit of both parties. 2) An exchange service of valuable information between generators and potential users of industrial and commercial wastes, whereby a beneficial use rather than disposal is the end result. This service identifies both the producers and potential markets for by- products, surpluses, unspent materials, and other forms of solid waste that are no longer needed.

A process that ranks waste management options according to what is most environmentally sound, giving top priority to preventing waste. The hierarchy from top to bottom is reduce, reuse, recycle, recovery, and disposal.

An expert worker in a lean manufacturing environment who shifts between workstations and provides auxiliary assistance as needed to maintain production flow. The water spider knows all processes well enough to take over if necessary.
A project management methodology using structured, linear phases to complete tasks. Each phase flows sequentially into the next, resembling a waterfall.

A method of selecting and sequencing picking lists or items to minimize the waiting time of the delivered material. Shipping orders may be picked in waves combined by common carrier or destination, and items for manufacturing orders may be picked in waves based on required work centers.

A document accompanying a shipment containing a list of the goods being transported, instructions related to the shipment, the shipment origin and destination, and the shipper and recipient. See: air waybill (AWB).

Paths over which a carrier operates, including right-of- way, roadbed, tracks, and other physical facilities. These may be owned by the government, privately held by the carrier, or provided by nature.

A form of technology worn on the body that allows hands-free work by being voice and/or gesture activated. Wearables can be used for a wide variety of activities within a supply chain, including tracking activity levels, distances moved to execute transactions, and even the exact location of workers in the warehouse.
A list of web pages that is structured hierarchically.
A single document that is accessible on the internet and contains hypertext links to other documents and files. See: uniform resource locator (URL).

A common internet or intranet framework that enables the movement of data from one supply chain application to another, without the requirement for a direct connection between the two applications and without regard to the underlying operating system for those applications.
Syn.: push technology.
The process of confirming a shipment arrival only by confirming that the correct weight has been delivered.
The even spread of cargo weight on a trailer or other piece of transportation equipment to ensure safety and stability of the shipment while it is in transit.
An averaging technique in which the data to be averaged is not uniformly weighted but is given values according to its importance. See: moving average forecast, simple moving average.
Syn.: weighted-factor rating method.

A method used to analyze the advantages of various locations or other decision alternatives along several qualitative and quantitative dimensions that are weighted by their importance. Syn.: weighted scoring model.

A supplier selection and rating approach that uses the input gathered in the categorical plan approach and assigns weights to each evaluation category. A weighted sum for each supplier is obtained, and a comparison is made. The weights used should total 100 percent for all categories.
The process of evaluating alternative strategies by examining the consequences of changes to forecasts, manufacturing plans, inventory levels, etc. See: sensitivity analysis, simulation.
A wedge of sturdy material placed against a vehicle's wheel to prevent accidental movement.
A listing of every parent item that calls for a given component, and the respective quantity required, from the bill of material (BOM). See: implosion, indented where-used list, pegging.

A supply chain intermediary that buys products from many manufacturers and distributors and sells them to retailers. A wholesaler primarily works to satisfy the needs of retailers as opposed to a distributor, which works closely with a manufacturer to market its products.
A public or private data communication system for linking computers distributed over a large geographic area.
A service process that allows customers to walk up to the seller’s facility and pick up the items they have previously ordered.
Acronym for work in process.
1) Removal of material from stores. 2) A transaction issuing material to a specific location, run, or schedule.
An indicator that materials or components can be transported between work areas or storage locations.
Acronym for warehouse management system.

In project management, a hierarchical description of a project in which all tasks are listed, with each lower level being more detailed. The WBS is used to determine resource needs, timelines, and costs.
Dissimilar machines grouped together into a production unit to produce a family of parts having similar routings. See: cellular layout, cellular manufacturing, U-shaped layout.

A specific production area, consisting of one or more people and/or machines with similar capabilities, that can be considered as one unit for purposes of capacity requirements planning (CRP) and detailed scheduling. Syn.: load center.
A file that contains information about a specific work center, such as capacity information, hours worked per shift, shifts worked, utilization, and efficiency.
Syn.: dispatch list.
A listing of every manufactured item that is routed to a given work center either as a primary or secondary routing.

A good in various stages of completion throughout the plant, including all material from raw material that has been released for initial processing up to completely processed material awaiting final inspection and acceptance as finished goods inventory. Many accounting systems also include the value of semi-finished stock and components in this category. Syn.: in-process inventory.
Documentation of the steps required to perform a task or tasks within a process. See: process sheet.
The analysis of the time it takes a qualified worker to complete a task, job, or activity according to an established level of performance. See: standard time.

1) An order to the machine shop for tool manufacture or equipment maintenance. This is not to be confused with a manufacturing order. Syn.: work ticket. 2) An authorization to start work on an activity (e.g., maintenance) or product. See: manufacturing order.

In project management, a set of tasks at the lowest level of a work breakdown structure (WBS) that produce a specific deliverable outcome. This may be treated as a subproject to be assigned to a project manager to plan and execute, in which case this manager will define new activities.
The use of random samples to determine the frequency with which certain activities are performed.
A set of activities ordered to accomplish work.
A group of employees established to oversee a work area or function.
Syn.: work order.

A project management technique that provides a response to a negative risk or event that has happened. A workaround is different from a contingency plan because a workaround is not planned before the risk event occurs.
A measure (usually computed as a percentage) of worker performance that compares the standard time allowed to complete a task with the actual worker time to complete it. Syn.: labor efficiency.
The value of total goods and services produced by an employee divided by the labor hours required to produce those goods and services.
Syn.: net working capital.
Syn.: cycle stock.
Syn.: load.

The arrangement of tools, equipment, materials, and supplies according to their frequency of use. Those items that are never used are removed from the workplace, and those items that are used frequently are located for fast, easy access and replacement. See: 5S.
The assigned location such as a machine or workbench where a worker performs a job. See: work center.
The successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and the current international agency overseeing trade between nations.
An organization that has reached a globally recognized level of excellence as a result of its consistently superior products or services and customer satisfaction.
The highest level of quality that an organization can achieve in its products, processes, or service.
In accounting, the process of removing an unrecoverable asset or bad debt from an organization’s balance sheet through the expensing process.
Acronym for World Trade Organization.
Syn.: average chart.
Abbreviation for extensible markup language.
A system that organizes and directs the traffic of all vehicles in the parking yards located at various industrial buildings like warehouses, distribution centers (DCs), and manufacturing plants.
An introductory credential that recognizes a person's foundational knowledge of six sigma concepts, tools, and methodology.
The middle-level buffer zone in drum-buffer-rope scheduling where the yellow color is used to indicate cautious situation of buffer consumption.

The amount of good or acceptable material available after the completion of a process. It is usually computed as the amount of acceptable output divided by the initial production quantity. In manufacturing planning and control systems, yield is often used to determine how many units should be scheduled to generate a specific number of acceptable units. Syns.: material yield, process yield. See: scrap factor.
A measurement of the yield of a process. For a specific process or operation, yield factor plus scrap factor equals 1.
A dynamic pricing strategy that organizations use to maximize total profit. It is typically applied in situations where available product or resources are constrained.
Acronym for yard management system.
A Japanese word referring to the sharing of knowledge and best practices throughout an organization to allow for other departments to benefit from organizational learning.
A lean strategy that challenges organizations to strive to eliminate errors and flaws in its operations through preventative measures rather than inspecting output and correcting defects.

1) A lean strategy focused on reducing the need for maintaining excess inventory by establishing stability and consistency in the production process and minimizing waste, enabling the firm to match demand with supply effectively. See: just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing. 2) In retail operations, a business model in which online retailers do not stock products and instead have them shipped from suppliers directly to customers. See: drop shipping.

A budget procedure used primarily by governmental agencies in which managers are required to newly justify each budgetary expenditure as if the budget were being initiated for the first time, rather than being based on an adjustment of prior-year data.

1) A warehouse location methodology that includes some of the characteristics of fixed and random location methods. Zone locations hold certain kinds of items, depending on physical characteristics or frequency of use. 2) The specific warehouse location assigned to an order picker under a zone picking strategy.

A method of subdividing a picking list by areas within a storeroom for more efficient and rapid order picking. In picking items for an order, the picker retrieves only the items for each order that are located within his or her zone. The picker then moves to the next zone and continues picking the order or transfers the order to the next zone's picker. See: batch picking, discrete order picking, order picking.
A standard product price that applies to all geographic locations within a zone.
